TWO UNBOUNDED SETS, TWO POLICIES, and the asymmetry is the point: an audit file for a live workspace is worth keeping at any age, a journal for a dead workspace is worthless at any size. SET 1, THE AUDIT LOG HAD NO ROTATION AT ALL: store.rs gave the journal a full discipline (512 KiB gate, RETENTION_LINES 5000, RETENTION_GENS 4, RETENTION_BYTES 5 MiB, generations, an audit row per drop) while file_host::append_audit_row was a bare OpenOptions::append + writeln!. Exactly backwards, because the audit log records every PER-ATTEMPT failure and is therefore the high-volume file and the one a repeating fault writes to. Measured: one stale-socket respawn loop grew flywheel-toron.audit.jsonl to 14 GB (65,512,446 rows of one identical failure), flywheel-flywheel to 11 GB, flywheel-beads to 1.4 GB, chiebukuro to 366 MB — 26 GB of doorbell state — while the journal that WAS bounded held 4705 rows. FIX: rotate_audit_if_oversized caps at 5 MiB keeping the newest 4000 rows, reads TAIL-ONLY because reading a 14 GB file to trim it would OOM the very daemon trying to stay up, and swaps via temp+rename so a crash mid-rotation leaves the original intact rather than a truncated one. Generations deliberately NOT used. SET 2, JOURNALS: one file per workspace the plane has EVER served, nothing ever removed any — and this was not only 20 MB. known_journal_workspaces reports one entry per file and that count IS known_workspaces, which feeds the standby wake-blind signal, so 913 stale files were a PERMANENT FALSE ALARM in /health for a fleet that no longer existed. FIX: prune_unhosted_workspace_logs on the EXISTING hourly rotate_tick (same tick that already copy-truncates the doorbell's own log; no new timer, no new cadence), requiring BOTH not-currently-hosted AND mtime older than 7 days. The age gate is what makes deleting live state safe: a just-spawned crew whose host loop has not written yet is never a candidate, so a live workspace's journal — its wake record — cannot be removed. The threshold is generous because the failure modes are not symmetric: too eager deletes a live crew's wake record, too late only costs a file. PruneReport counts journals_removed, bytes_freed, skipped_young and remove_failed and is logged, because a prune that cannot report what it did is how a retention policy becomes a mystery. FENCES: 6 for the audit cap (one written at real ~6 MiB scale so the tail-only read is the path that runs, one pinning that rotation keeps the NEWEST rows and newline-terminates every one because a partial tail row is corrupted by the next append, one that a healthy log is not rewritten on every append, one fencing the constant itself) and 3 for the prune (all three cases in one test — unhosted+old goes, HOSTED+old stays, unhosted+young stays — plus idempotence, plus a bystander notes.jsonl that must survive so the prune cannot delete a shape it does not understand). FALSIFIED: disabling rotation reds the scale test; keeping the OLDEST rows reds the direction test; removing the live-workspace guard and removing the age gate each red the prune safety test INDEPENDENTLY. LIVE after install and restart: degraded reduced to ['journal_torn_tail'] alone, with watch_restart_loop, standby_with_known_workspaces AND inbox_fetch_failing all GONE; known_workspaces 858 -> 257 because the prune ran AT STARTUP (tokio::time::interval fires its first tick immediately); watch.last_event_age_s 6; injection.injectable 5; doorbell state 26 GB -> 516 KB; journals 20 MB -> 16 MB; largest audit file 28 KB. 171 doorbell-rt and 70 doorbell-cli tests pass. FIXTURE CORRECTION recorded because it nearly became a false finding: the first prune fence passed a logical 'now' in 2033, making a file written seconds earlier look decades old and removing TWO files instead of one. The assertion was right and my fixture was wrong; it now uses real time so the age relationship it asserts is real. PRINCIPLES: fix-root-causes — a retention policy that omits the highest-volume file is not a policy, and an unbounded counter feeding an alarm is a false alarm forever; prove-it-works — every guard is falsifiable independently, including the two that make DELETING live state safe, because an unfalsifiable guard is not a guard.

title: judgment stages: composable preflight/inflight checks, with Code/Jev/Compose and a first-class Unknown
description:
A judgment STAGE is a named, individually skippable check that runs at a stated point in a
workflow. This makes the ONE Jev call that existed (the crew-menu ranker) the first member of a
shape that can hold several, which is what "compose preflight and/or inflight" requires.

THREE STAGE KINDS, and `Code` is not a consolation prize.

  Stage::Code     a plain predicate, NO network
  Stage::Jev      a pack of questions + a code-side threshold
  Stage::Compose  several stages under Rule::{All, Any, Majority}

`Code` exists so that a check the compiler can already answer does not become a 5-second HTTP
call. Most of the real defects found this session were decidable in Rust: does this verify
command match zero tests, is this wave held, is this binding commit unique. Wiring any of those
as a Jev stage would be paying latency to learn something known, which is the "Jev is
load-bearing" failure the ranker's own module doc refuses. A stage that Jev adds nothing to must
be EXPRESSIBLE as Code so the registry can honestly say so.

crew-fit is now Compose{ All, [Code(menu-contested), Jev(crew-fit:rank)] }. A one-option menu is
decided in Rust and never reaches the network, and that saving is a visible property of the
composition rather than an `if` buried in the function that also does the ranking.

WHY UNKNOWN IS FIRST-CLASS, which is the whole design.

Signal::{Holds, Fails, Unknown}. `Unknown` is not an error variant: no key, transport error,
malformed answer, or a value below the stage's own floor. Callers handle it by falling back. The
property that makes this safe is that an unanswered stage is never indistinguishable from a
refusal — collapse those two and a network outage masquerades as a decision. `Verdict` keeps
Unavailable distinct from Reject for exactly that reason.

THE BUG THE LIVE RUN FOUND IN THIS DESIGN, which is the reason the seam is written down.

The first cut mapped a ranker's `Declined` to `Signal::Fails`. The live briefing duly reported

    jev declined: menu-contested=Holds, crew-fit:rank=Fails

Under `Rule::All` one Fails makes the parent Fails, and `verdict_of` turns that into
`Verdict::Reject`. Nothing gated on it at the time, so it was a LATENT refusal — but the moment
anything gates on a verdict, a shrug (every score below the confidence floor) would have become a
DISPATCH REFUSAL. A decline now maps to `Unknown`, which is what "no signal" means, and
`a_decline_is_never_a_failure_so_a_shrug_can_never_refuse_a_dispatch` fences it on the signal and
the resulting verdict rather than on wording.

`Verdict::Escalate` was DELETED rather than shipped: `verdict_of` had no producer for it, so it
was a variant an operator would read as "escalation is implemented". It returns when a stage can
produce it.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT TAKEN.

- No second request for crew-fit. The documented rank-wide/re-read-top-few/reject-all shape pays
  off when the roster is large and the summaries are lossy (182 skills truncated to 60 chars). A
  crew menu is 2-5 options whose full state already fits, so a second round trip re-reads text
  that was never truncated. The stage shape does not change when the menu grows; only the packs
  inside it do.
- No arithmetic in any criterion string. Jev does not count reliably and is not a calculator, so
  every sum, threshold, and comparison is Rust. That is why `read` returns a Signal computed in
  code rather than a number for a later stage to weigh.
- `assemble` stays pure. The model call lives in a named stage, so where the menu's options came
  from stays auditable. A model call inside the deriver would put an unauditable input inside the
  auditable function.

Gates: clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings exits 0. fmt clean. 19 tests across
stage:: and jev_rank::. Live `flywheel briefing` reports
"jev unavailable (menu-contested=Holds, crew-fit:rank=Unknown): deterministic order" and the
deterministic order stands, which is the property that matters.
close_reason: Judgment stages landed: Stage::{Code,Jev,Compose} with Rule::{All,Any,Majority} and a first-class Signal::Unknown, so an unanswered stage can never be mistaken for a refusal. crew-fit is the first real stage and is a Compose of a Code guard (a one-option menu never reaches the network) plus the Jev rank. The live run caught a bug in this design — a decline mapped to Fails, which under Rule::All reached Verdict::Reject, i.e. a shrug would have refused a dispatch — and it is now Unknown and fenced on the signal and the verdict. Verdict::Escalate deleted rather than shipped with no producer.

title: Dispatch-time registry does not carry the crew that was just spawned, so every @role lookup misses
description:
The root cause behind 'pane dispatch: no crew pane for @oracle' and the reason neither a bigger crew nor a bounded settle helps. Found by live test on 2026-09-27, not by reading.

Evidence: 'flywheel steer --project toron --crew 5' spawns five crew panes — the run's own final pane list holds crew-goal-coder, crew-goal-housekee, crew-goal-oracle, crew-goal-planner, crew-goal-reviewer — and the goal workflow's five steps need exactly those roles. The dispatch still fails, and its 'spawned:' list names only four entries, omitting housekeeper and oracle.

Meanwhile the on-disk spawn registry for the project, ~/.local/state/flywheel/agents/flywheel-toron.json, holds ONE row and it is unrelated (flywheel-toron-pi2, profile=None, pane w0:p2). None of the five crew panes were persisted there. The project mirror .flywheel/agent-names.json is from Sep 22 and holds 3 stale rows.

So the crew exists only in the in-memory value spawn_crew_into returns for the run, while the dispatch path resolves @role against a registry loaded from disk (live_registry_for_dispatch, src/pane.rs:90-98, which calls crate::state::load_spawn_registry). A freshly spawned crew is invisible to the resolver that must dispatch to it. The 4 entries the error does list are consistent with the in-memory set minus the two roles whose rows were never written.

This also explains why the failure is immune to crew size: at --crew 3 the packer folds oracle and housekeeper onto coder (bd-8c5h, a second and independent fault), and at --crew 5 nothing folds but the rows still never reach the registry this bead is about.

Fix: make the crew the run just spawned the thing the dispatcher resolves against. Persist each spawned pane to the registry at spawn time, or pass the in-memory crew registry through to the dispatch call instead of re-loading from disk. Whichever is chosen, the resolver and the spawner must share one source of truth; a resolver that reads a store the spawner does not write cannot ever find a new pane.

Acceptance: after 'flywheel steer --project toron --crew 5', the project spawn registry contains all five crew rows, and a dispatch to any of the five roles resolves without a settle or a bail. A test proves a pane spawned by the run is resolvable by its @role at dispatch time.
close_reason: status: disproven, not fixed; no product code changed for this bead. The premise was that the dispatch-time registry does not carry the crew the run just spawned. Live measurement during a running crew-5 steer on 2026-09-27 refuted it: the project registry held all six rows (EmberOtter, crew-goal-coder, crew-goal-housekee, crew-goal-oracle, crew-goal-planner, crew-goal-reviewer) and spawn_crew_into persists them at src/pane.rs:895. My earlier one-row reading was taken after the run had been reaped, so I measured a post-teardown state and drew a wrong conclusion from a real file. Closed as disproven so the next agent does not chase it, with the measurement rule recorded as a learning at docs/learnings/measure-during-the-run-not-after-reap.md. PRINCIPLES: prove-it-works — the live registry read inside the run window is the artifact, and it contradicted my reading taken outside it; encode-lessons-in-structure — the reap-window rule is a doc anyone can re-run, not a note in a bead thread.

title: flywheel decide: pure classifier + table tests (captain SM)
description:
NEW file src/decide.rs (genuinely new). Pure decide() — no IO.

pub struct Snapshot { pub ready_bead_count: u32, pub profiled_panes: u32, pub launch_pending: u32, pub contention: bool }
pub struct Decision { pub primitive: &'static str, pub reason: String, pub argv: Vec<String> }
pub fn decide(target: &str, snap: &Snapshot) -> Decision

Table (target substring + snap → primitive):
- target contains audit|read-only|analyze AND not implement/fix → captain-audit (headless workflow run)
- snap.ready_bead_count>0 AND target empty or work|loop|beads → loop-work
- implement|fix + beads|tracker|gate → steer
- implement|fix + no tracker|direct → steer-direct
- compose|catalog miss|parts: → compose-parts
- shape unknown|improvise|author workflow → compose-agent
- contention|coalition|shared-file → coalition-form

title: pane dispatch has no wait-for-idle gate, so a multi-stage workflow exhausts retries and trips the breaker
description:
Found while steering a 3-agent wave-swarm crew (bd-qlr1). Reproducible: flywheel workflow compose --parts wave-swarm --crew 'rust-coder:1,coder:1,reviewer:1' (all harnesses pi) spawns 3 agents on 3 panes and dispatches 6 stage prompts, then fails with 'pane dispatch: consecutive-failure breaker Open'. Four consecutive runs, same shape.

Mechanism, verified by reading the code: wave-swarm has 7 stages (gate, dispatch, execute, observe, review, verify, compound, signoff) mapped onto 3 agents, so each agent receives 2-3 prompts back to back. is_transient_dispatch_reason (src/pane.rs) treats agent_not_ready and agent_pane_busy as transient, so the 2nd send to an agent that is already 'working' retries 6 times with dispatch_policy.delay_for backoff totalling roughly 5s intervals. A busy agent stays busy for MINUTES, so all 6 retries fail, the dispatch records a breaker failure, and after 5 the ConsecutiveBreaker opens and every later step fast-escalates. The visible error is only the breaker message, which hides the real cause.

Corroboration: a 2-part compose ('--parts coder:ce-execute --parts reviewer:ce-review') with ONE prompt per agent lands reliably, including the opencode reviewer. The difference is exactly prompts-per-agent.

herdr's own agent.start help names the fix and flywheel is not using it: 'next: herdr agent prompt <TARGET> <TEXT> --wait', documented as avoiding a race between separate calls. flywheel instead does agent_wait/agent_start and then a separate dispatch, which is the documented race.

Fix direction: before a send to a pane that already has a working agent, wait for that agent to return to Idle (bounded, with the readiness reason surfaced), rather than treating 'busy' as a 5-second transient. Do NOT simply lengthen the retries - a busy agent needs a readiness wait, not more attempts. Keep the breaker as the backstop. Also consider surfacing the first underlying reason in the escalated error so the breaker message stops hiding the cause.
close_reason:
bd-5llv fixed in 3397053. The real root cause was neither of the two things I proposed earlier in this bead, and both of my intermediate hypotheses were wrong. Recording the actual chain so nobody re-derives it.

THE BUG. The breaker decides success with out["ok"] == Some(true). The receipt was built with the verdict NESTED under "send", and top-level "ok" was written ONLY on the failure path:

    let mut out = json!({ "profile":..., "agent":..., "send": v.clone() });
    if v.get("ok") == Some(false) { ...; out["ok"] = json!(false); }

A landed send therefore produced a receipt with NO top-level "ok" at all. The comparison evaluated to None != Some(true), the else branch ran, and pane_dispatch recorded a BREAKER FAILURE for a dispatch that had SUCCEEDED. The breaker charged once per dispatch regardless of outcome and opened after five.

That is why the DISPATCH COUNT predicted failure rather than the result. wave-swarm makes 6 dispatches and always tripped it; the 2-prompt compose never reached 5 and always passed. It also explains the pane-liveness timeline (agents working, every prompt landed) and why the error blamed an unavailable pane when no pane was ever unavailable.

HOW IT WAS FOUND. Instrumenting all three record_failure_at sites (pane.rs 1180 retries-exhausted, 1320 not-ok, 1343 non-json-stdout) with a one-line marker. Only 1320 fired, and its payload was {"send":{"landed":true,"ok":true,...}} with no top-level ok. That is the whole diagnosis in one line. Instrument the sites rather than inferring a fourth mechanism from the outside.

WHAT I GOT WRONG ON THE WAY, so it is not repeated:
- First hypothesis: a mid-run reaper killed the panes. Wrong. main.rs:25661 is the END-of-run ephemeral reap; the workspace vanishing at t+15s was a consequence of the run failing fast.
- Second hypothesis: the transient classification was unreachable because a busy agent makes __send return Err with empty stdout. Wrong. prompt_coded (toron-core/src/backend/herdr.rs:910) never returns Err, it maps client errors to Ok(PromptLanding{code}), and pane_dispatch passes --confirm so it is on the confirm path where ok is always present. The error:agent_not_ready reason even contains the transient substring, so it WAS being retried correctly.
- What was actually true: being correctly classified transient and then exhausting MAX_ATTEMPTS is itself a breaker failure (site 1180). A busy agent is a ~5s-transient problem that needs a minutes-long wait, so the retry budget was guaranteed to be exhausted. Both a symptom (breaker charged per success) and a cause (busy agents burn the whole retry budget) were real and both are now fixed.

FIXES.
1. dispatch_receipt_ok carries the verdict's ok at the top level ALWAYS, so the breaker reads the verdict rather than the absence of a failure marker. A verdict with no ok still reads false, so an unexpected shape surfaces as a failure rather than a silent pass.
2. An idle gate before sending: wait up to 600s (10x the entire ~30s transient budget, still bounded) for the target to go Idle, because a working agent cannot be un-worked by retrying harder. On timeout, refuse naming the real cause, and deliberately do NOT charge the breaker: the breaker stops hammering an unavailable PANE, whereas sending too many prompts to one agent is a workflow-shape problem.

TESTS. 3 receipt + 3 idle-gate. Mutation-verified: re-introducing the old receipt shape fails exactly the 3 receipt tests and leaves the 3 independent idle-gate tests green, which is the evidence the regression test has teeth on the right thing. 1894 pass / 0 fail, clippy clean.

STILL OPEN, and now VISIBLE rather than hidden: wave-swarm's 7 stages fan several prompts onto each of 3 agents, so an agent gets a second prompt while still working on the first. The run now fails honestly with "was still busy after 600s - refusing to send a second prompt into an agent that has not finished the first", naming @coder as the failed step. That is a genuine structural mismatch, not a bug in the gate: an agent turn on this work exceeds 10 minutes, so a stage-per-agent workflow cannot reuse one agent for gate/dispatch/execute. Operator decision needed - one agent per concurrent stage, or combine a stage's prompts into a single send. Not decided here, and deliberately not worked around.

comments.author: bangedorrunt
comments.text:
MECHANISM SHARPENED, with a measured pane-liveness timeline and a likely third defect. Read before implementing.

MEASURED (poll of 'herdr workspace list' every 3s during a live 3-agent wave-swarm run):
  t+03s  w1E appears, panes=2, agents=idle
  t+06s  panes=3, idle
  t+09s  panes=3, agents=WORKING   <- prompts injected, agents ALIVE and working
  t+12s  panes=3, working
  t+15s  w1E GONE
So the agents did receive their prompts and were working. The workspace then disappears ~6s later. Correction to an earlier hypothesis of mine: that is NOT a mid-run reaper — src/main.rs:25661 is the END-of-run ephemeral reap, so the workspace vanishing at t+15s means the RUN ENDED at t+15s. The vanishing is a consequence of the fast failure, not an independent reaper. Operator observed the same thing independently ('3 panes, vanished once prompt injected').

LIKELY THIRD DEFECT, the one to check first: the transient classification is UNREACHABLE on the error path. In pane_dispatch (src/pane.rs ~1050-1250) the flow is:

  if let Ok(v) = serde_json::from_str(trimmed) { ... is_transient_dispatch_reason(v[reason]) ... }
  ...
  // non-JSON stdout falls through to:
  dispatch_breaker().lock().record_failure_at(...); return Ok(out with ok:false);

is_transient_dispatch_reason is only consulted INSIDE the successful-parse branch, and it reads the parsed 'reason' field. But cmd_internal_send (src/main.rs ~28500) returns Err — printing NOTHING to stdout — when the send errors, including when the agent_not_ready retry-by-pane-id ALSO fails (backend.prompt_coded(...)? propagates). An Err from __send means empty stdout, so the caller cannot classify it as transient at all: it hard-fails AND records a breaker failure. A busy agent therefore takes the one path guaranteed to open the breaker.

That is consistent with every observation: agents working, six dispatches, only ONE 'not ready (attempt 1/6)' line logged (the transient path), and the breaker opening after five.

CHECK FIRST: does a resolved (non-Err) __send verdict for a BUSY agent carry reason 'agent_not_ready'/'agent_pane_busy' (transient, retried), or does herdr return an error code for a busy agent (non-JSON, hard fail)? If the latter, the fix is to make __send always emit its verdict JSON on the agent_not_ready/busy paths instead of returning Err, so the existing transient classification can see it. Do not paper over it by lengthening retries.

comments.author: bangedorrunt
comments.text:
RETRACTION of my own "likely third defect" above. It is WRONG. Do not implement it.

What I claimed: the transient classification is unreachable because a busy agent makes __send return Err, printing nothing to stdout, so is_transient_dispatch_reason is never consulted and every such dispatch hard-fails plus records a breaker failure.

Why it is wrong, verified by reading the code:

1. pane_dispatch DOES pass --confirm, and confirm: Option<u64> is declared with num_args = 0..=1 and default_missing_value = "45000", so a bare --confirm is Some(45000), NOT a clap usage error.
2. So __send takes the CONFIRM path, not the legacy fire-and-forget path. The legacy path (confirm_ms == None) is the only one that can return Err on a busy agent, and pane_dispatch never uses it.
3. On the confirm path both attempts go through backend.prompt_coded (main.rs around 28549 and 28554). prompt_coded (toron-core/src/backend/herdr.rs:910) NEVER returns Err - it maps every client error into Ok(PromptLanding { status: None, code: Some(code) }). The question-mark on those calls therefore never propagates.
4. So a busy agent yields SendVerdict::Coded("agent_not_ready"), then confirm_send_json, then {"ok": true, "landed": false, "reason": "error:agent_not_ready"}.
5. is_transient_dispatch_reason does a substring contains, and "error:agent_not_ready" CONTAINS "agent_not_ready", so it IS classified transient and IS retried.
6. And because that body has ok:true, the breaker branch calls record_success_at(), not record_failure_at().

Net consequence: a busy agent CANNOT open the breaker. My explanation for the 5 breaker failures was wrong, and the real cause is still OPEN. Do not spend effort on the emit-JSON-on-error idea.

STILL ESTABLISHED (keep these):

- @role is single-target: resolve_pane_entry (pane.rs:152) matches profile and returns ONE entry via best_generation. A crew of N sharing a role name sends every dispatch to one pane. Workaround that works: give each agent a DISTINCT role name, e.g. --crew "rust-coder:1,coder:1,reviewer:1". Verified: crew 3 member(s), 3 panes, dispatches fan out.
- Prompts-per-agent is the variable that separates working from failing. One prompt per agent (a 2-part compose) lands reliably including the opencode reviewer. wave-swarm's 7 stages onto 3 agents means 2-3 prompts each, and it always fails.
- The pane-liveness timeline (agents working at t+09s, workspace gone at t+15s) shows the agents DID receive prompts. The workspace vanishing is the END-of-run ephemeral reap at main.rs:25661 firing because the run failed fast, NOT a mid-run reaper.
- The visible error is only the breaker message, which hides the underlying reason. That is still true and still worth fixing.

NEXT STEP, and it must come before any fix: capture what pane_dispatch actually receives. The breaker needs 5 record_failure calls, and with ok:true on every confirmed send the only remaining sites are pane.rs:1246 (stdout not parseable as JSON) and the post-MAX_ATTEMPTS path at pane.rs:1083. So either __send is emitting non-JSON on some path, or dispatches are exhausting 6 transient retries and landing in the 1083 branch. Distinguish those two by logging the raw __send stdout and exit for one failing dispatch, rather than inferring it a fourth time. The agent.prompt probe over the herdr socket kept blocking on recv, so prefer instrumenting pane_dispatch's existing eprintln path (it already has raw and err in scope) over writing a new socket client.

title: journal() burns a seq before the append and discards the error, so a lost row becomes a permanent unexplained gap
description:
Live evidence, 2026-09-27: doorbell-journal-flywheel-opencode.jsonl is contiguous through 4,633 sequenced rows except one hole. Line 3256 is seq 153410 at 07:32:24Z, line 3257 is seq 153427 at 07:32:41Z. Those 16 seq values (153411-153426) exist in NO journal file on disk (checked every file in ~/.local/state/flywheel/journals), and no row anywhere is missing a seq field. Both sides of the hole are the Sweep cadence at one row per second, so the sweeps kept ticking through a 17-second window and each tick consumed a seq and left nothing behind.

Mechanism, crates/doorbell-rt/src/brain.rs journal(): 'let seq = self.next_seq; self.next_seq += 1; let _ = self.store.append_journal_seq(...)'. The seq advances BEFORE the write and the write's error is thrown away, so any failing append burns a seq permanently and reports nothing at the time. The gap is the only trace, it is unexplainable from the journal, and /health reduces it to one boolean (journal_torn_tail) which also STOPS the fold at the tear, hiding every row after it from 'doorbell why'.

Most plausible cause of the unwritable window: rotate() rewrites the active file with std::fs::write(&active, ...) - a truncate-and-rewrite from a snapshot, not an append - and drops rows by design while its doc comment claims 'Every drop is an audit row'. That file contains no rotation row at all.

Fix direction: do not consume a seq you did not write; make a lost row name itself (counter + a journal_write_failed audit carrying the seq); make rotation's drops carry the seq range they removed; and consider keeping the fold going past a tear while reporting how much it withheld. NOTE: a gap is evidence - closing it silently would make the loss invisible, so the fix is to NAME it, not to hide it.

Evidence written up in docs/learnings/doorbell/died-storm-620-per-second.md (bd-455x).

comments.author: CopperWren
comments.text:
ESCALATION: row loss is systemic, not a one-off. A contiguity scan of every journal in ~/.local/state/flywheel/journals found gaps on SEVEN workspaces, not one:
- doorbell-journal-flywheel-chiebukuro.jsonl: 89 gaps in 4,939 rows, including ONE JUMP OF 5,175 consecutive seqs (1379399 -> 1384574) and another of 273 (1386153 -> 1386426).
- toron.dev: 5 gaps. dotfiles: 6 gaps. torondev: 2 gaps. flywheel-chiebukuro, flywheel-toron, opencode: 1 gap each (18, 18, 16 seqs).
The generation files (.1-.4) hold one row each, so the missing seqs are not parked in an archive: they are gone from disk entirely. Every one of these files contains ZERO rotation/trim rows, so a rotation drop is never audited despite rotate()'s doc comment claiming 'Every drop is an audit row'.
Consequence for health honesty: the fold stops at the first tear, so each of these workspaces reports journal_torn_tail forever. The flag is not a false positive (rows really are gone) but it is permanently red on the busiest workspaces, which is the same 'a signal that is always on says nothing' failure as the RestartWatch metric was.
Implication for this bead: the fix is bigger than guarding a failed append. Rotation removes rows from the middle of the seq stream on purpose, unaudited, and the fold cannot tell a designed drop from a torn write. Until the drop names its seq range, every tear is unattributable.

CORRECTION to my escalation comment above, then what is left here.

I had grepped the journal file and concluded the audit did not exist. Same class of error as the shed/cause claim: I reasoned about the wrong artifact.

No record covers that range, so those 16 seqs are not retention: a lost write, exactly this bead. chiebukuro is the opposite and worse: 89 gaps (one of 5,175 seqs), four generation files on disk so rotation ran, and the sum of its recorded dropped_lines is ZERO. principles.decision: a size cap on a spinning writer converts unbounded disk growth into unbounded CPU, so the write RATE must be bounded too

title: Doorbell CPU/memory/disk leak: restart storm, retention amplification, and test writes into the live state dir
description:
Doorbell disk/CPU/memory leak, and the test suite writing into the live state dir.

LEDGER NOTE FIRST, because the audit trail should not be quietly tidied: the token
`bd-lorot` was cited in six commits (684ebb5, a924c1f, 3f64714, 1b0998b, ece619d,
21f581e) but no such bead existed. The commit guard checks only that a
`bd-*` token appears in the message, not that the bead resolves, so the gap was
invisible to it. This bead is the real record; the id does not match the cited
one and that mismatch is deliberate to surface rather than hide.

THE INCIDENT, measured. doorbell serve ran at 184% CPU and 679 MB RSS. The chain,
each link counted rather than inferred:
- flywheel-flywheel.audit.jsonl grew at 169 KB/s = 1,408 identical
  `wake_sock_absent` rows per SECOND (timestamp-bucketed).
- Each burst crossed the 5 MiB cap, so the rotation rewrote the file continuously.
  The retention fix became the AMPLIFIER: faithfully rewriting a file a spin loop
  fed. A bound on size is necessary and not sufficient; the write RATE needs a
  bound too.
- The root: `restart_wake` had a correct escalating backoff and NO single-flight
  guard, so every `Died` scheduled its own timer. 1,408 timers each slept 16s
  and all fired together. A backoff spaces ONE retry; without single-flight it is
  not a rate limit.
- The casualty: those queued connections drove the toron daemon to EMFILE
  (`accept error: Too many open files`, 234 fds on wake.sock), killing the accept
  loop and the very socket the doorbell was polling. Two services took each other
  down.

FIXES, each with a fence proven red by neutering the guarded thing:
- single-flight on the restart (51 deaths scheduled 51 restarts without it; the
  flag must also REOPEN or a later outage is never retried)
- the absence audited once per outage, not once per attempt
- SIGTERM-before-SIGKILL is not in this repo; see toron bd-yolv
- orphaned liveness stamps (`watch-<ws>.hb` / `.event`) pruned on the same two
  guards as journals. My first fence for this passed for the WRONG reason: I aged
  only the dead workspace's stamps, so the hosted guard was never exercised. A
  fence that passes for the wrong reason is worse than none.
- `journal_torn_tail` scoped to HOSTED workspaces: an unhosted workspace's frozen
  journal cannot affect delivery, so it cannot evidence a delivery fault, yet it
  held `degraded` red permanently. Plus the LoudMiss row de-duplicated — it
  re-fired every few seconds forever, which is noise that trains a reader to skip
  the field.
- the whole facts plane threaded with an EXPLICIT state root and deliberately NO
  default wrapper: adding the parameter broke 11 call sites at compile time, which
  is the guarantee working. The default was the trap.
- test cleanup removed entirely rather than moved — cleaning the live tree from a
  test is the bug wearing a tidy hat.

RESULT, live, on the installed binary: CPU 184% -> 1.8%, RSS 679MB -> 31MB, audit
1408 rows/s -> 0 in 6s, toron fds 234 -> 38, socket ConnectionRefused -> CONNECT
OK, last_event_age_s 377 -> 11, and `degraded` went from 3 items to [].

FOLLOW-UP NOT DONE HERE: toron bd-yolv (the 72 orphaned resonate serve processes
that caused the fd exhaustion in the first place) is a separate repo and a
separate bead.
close_reason: Fixed and proven live. doorbell 184% CPU / 679 MB -> 1.8% / 31 MB; audit 1408 rows/s -> 0; toron fds on wake.sock 234 -> 38; socket refused -> CONNECT OK; last_event_age_s 377 -> 11; degraded 3 -> []; 5-min soak flat. Causes: (1) restart_wake had a correct backoff and NO single-flight guard, so N deaths scheduled N timers -- a backoff spaces ONE retry -- and the storm drove the toron daemon to EMFILE, killing the socket the doorbell was polling, so the two services took each other down; (2) the 5 MiB retention cap became the amplifier, faithfully rewriting a file a spin loop fed, so the write RATE needed bounding too; (3) orphaned liveness stamps and an UNHOSTED workspace's torn journal both degraded a live daemon; (4) the LoudMiss row re-fired every few seconds forever; (5) the facts plane read an ambient state_dir inside the seam, so tests inherited the live root -- now an explicit parameter with no default wrapper. LEDGER: implementation commits cite bd-lorot, never a real bead; the guard checks the token appears, not that it resolves. Real bead bd-6rtl.

comments.author: bangedorrunt
comments.text:
Taking this over with operator permission. The AGENTS.md audit (2026-09-22) left
this bead "conditional" and named the two remaining gaps. I located both, with
line numbers, rather than restating the audit.

GAP 1 — ambient RuntimeAuthority. `RuntimeAuthority::resolve()` has 12 call
sites. Nine are inside #[cfg(test)] modules, which is correct and not the gap:
  src/workspace.rs 6319, 6365, 6641, 6679  (tests)
  src/durable.rs 6010                        (test)
  src/main.rs 10043, 13109, 24724, 25454    (tests)
Three are PRODUCTION, and these are the "legacy Jev helpers":
  src/cmd/judgment.rs:382, :402   both inside cmd_judgment — the judgment
                                  annotate/pre-screen doors
  src/doorbell_host.rs:191        inside `fn new`
A constructor and a CLI door that each resolve their own authority cannot be
given a substituted one, so neither can be driven by a test with a fake
authority. That is the exact shape the Tick Law forbids one layer up: host
policy entering through an ambient read instead of arriving as data.

GAP 2 — ambient clock in a durable effect leaf. Exactly ONE production site,
not "several":
  src/durable.rs run_leaf_cmd_bounded (line 2104), Instant::now() at 2133 and
  2138, forming the watchdog deadline and polling it.
Everything else in durable.rs is already clean; I checked the whole file
against SystemTime::now / Instant::now / monotonic_now / unix_now and stopped
at the test module.

Read this one carefully before "fixing" it, because the obvious fix is wrong.
A subprocess watchdog MUST read a real monotonic clock: substitute a fake clock
and the deadline never arrives, the child is never killed, and the process hangs
forever. So the read is not the defect. The defect is the ABSENCE OF A SEAM.
Today the watchdog length and poll cadence are baked into the function body, so
no test can script the hang case the repo's own effect law demands ("an
interpreter test substitutes the clock... It scripts success, typed failure,
hang, and cancellation"). The law cannot currently be satisfied for this leaf at
any test cost.

Second defect in the same function, which the audit did not name: a timeout
returns a bare std::io::Error, which is the SAME type a spawn failure returns.
Success, typed failure, defect and interruption are supposed to stay distinct,
and "the child ignored SIGTERM and needed SIGKILL at the deadline" is a typed
domain outcome that currently cannot be told apart from "the binary was not
found". Callers cannot make a different decision for those two.

Planned fix, TDD first: (1) give the watchdog an injectable seam for its clock
and cadence, documented so a substituted clock may SHORTEN the watchdog but
never remove the real wait; (2) introduce a typed timeout outcome distinct from
spawn failure, keeping interruption distinct from both; (3) an interpreter test
that scripts success, typed failure, hang, and cancellation with no real sleep
of watchdog length.

title: a poisoned crate test lock made unrelated tests fail forever
description:
A `Mutex` is poisoned when a holder panics, and a poisoned lock stays poisoned for the life of the process. Five test sites took a crate-wide static lock with `.lock().unwrap()` rather than through a poison-tolerant accessor, so one unrelated panicking test turned every LATER test using that lock into a permanent `PoisonError` failure.

`judgment::tests::b5_find_pack_picks_highest_version` and `judgment::tests::xdg_pack_is_the_source_of_truth` were failing this way. Neither was broken; both were downstream of an unrelated panic holding `ENV_LOCK`, and both kept failing on every run thereafter. That is the worst shape of test failure: a real cascade that reads as a regression in code nobody touched.

`config::lock_env()` already recovered from poisoning and is documented as the reference pattern. The fix routes all five sites through poison-tolerant accessors, adding `verdict::lock_loop_reporter()` to mirror it for `LOOP_REPORTER_LOCK` (whose `LOOP_ARMED` flag is process-global, so the arming sequence runs many times per binary and a poisoned lock there is very costly).

A tripwire rejects any future `.lock().unwrap()` on a crate-wide static test lock. Per-test local mutexes are deliberately not flagged: poisoning one only breaks the single test that owns it.

## PRINCIPLES
fix-root-causes — the failure was lock poisoning propagating, so the fix is poison tolerance at every shared-lock site rather than repairing the two tests that happened to be downstream.

## VERIFY
```bash
mbx +nightly-aarch64-apple-darwin test -p flywheel --bin flywheel -- config::tests::no_test_takes_a_crate_wide_lock config::tests::the_env_lock_accessor judgment:: daemon::
```
close_reason: fix-root-causes — the failures were lock poisoning propagating, so the fix is poison tolerance at every shared-lock site rather than repairing whichever tests happened to be downstream.

title: the doorbell's wake model becomes a program on the framework
description:
ADR-0018 §3 step 3 (flywheel's half of the elm-effect port; the branch file is references/migrate-flywheel.md).

Doorbell ticks, herdr events and mail ingress become MESSAGES; they never call the model. The wake brain's state machine becomes a Program over the framework's Loop, with the model a pure fold and the interpreter at the edge.

The port module is flywheel's src/elm/ (the house convention: every plane keeps its framework adapter in a module named elm). The leaf adapter is already ported (bd-f572): a pure fold, Effect::sync at the edge, the framework's FileLog and Producer for the durable identity. This work ports the WAKE model on top of it.

The laws that bind it: the fold is pure (no clock, no environment, no store, no randomness in update); a dropped command value performs no I/O; the four outcomes stay apart (a defect is not the child's typed failure, and a cancelled run does not settle as a failed attempt); the model is a BTreeMap when its order changes the command list; the durable identity is the framework's (producer_id, epoch, seq) and the resume field is offset.

Also in scope, because it is the same plane: bd-3s2q (concurrent runs of one sender can land on the SAME epoch - the epoch must come from the run's own identity, not a counter two runs can share; it fails 3 of 6 runs at HEAD).

Done means: the wake brain's tick is a message into a pure fold, the interpreter runs the commands, and the epoch is unique per run - each with a test that goes red when the fix is inverted. The flywheel package suite must be green.
close_reason: The doorbell's models are ONE framework Program: the edges (a tick, a herdr event, a mail ingress) are messages, the fold is pure, the interpreter runs the commands at the edge, and the durable identity is the framework's (producer_id, epoch, seq) over a FileLog with the resume field as the offset. The fold DELEGATES to the core's one implementation (the dispatcher tick and the router tick), and the workspace's doorbell slice folds through the port's fold, so the live path and the program cannot drift. Eleven tests, each red when its fix is inverted (the interpreter, the defect mapping, the fold's delegation), plus the whole workspace suite green and a CLEAN EXPORT of the commit building and testing. prove-it-works - a test that goes red when the fix is inverted. fix-root-causes - the fold delegates instead of duplicating the decision. sequence-verifiable-units - the epoch fix lands first, the port on top of it. Residual: the doorbell DAEMON (crates/doorbell-rt) still runs its own fold - reaching the framework there is a toron_core::kernel dependency in a crate that deliberately carries no toron, and its brain mutates the model from the effect layer, which the interpreter shape forbids; the port's framework half is tested and ready, and the adoption is a decision, not a line.

title: collab drops a reply that lands before the watcher starts
description:
`flywheel collab` sends the ask, THEN starts `mail watch`, and the watcher records the thread's latest message as its baseline at startup. A reply that lands in that window becomes the baseline and is never reported, so collab reports a timeout for a thread that was answered.

Fix at the owner boundary: carry the OUTBOUND message id as the watch baseline instead of re-reading the thread head, so only a message newer than the ask can satisfy the wait. Standalone `mail watch` keeps its existing startup semantics (baseline = latest at start).

Second defect on the same path: `thread_id` is `collab-<UTC second>`, so two collabs started in the same second share a thread and cross-contaminate. Make it collision-resistant.

## PRINCIPLES
fix-root-causes — the lost reply is a baseline captured too late, not a timing flake.

## VERIFY
```bash
mbx +nightly-aarch64-apple-darwin test -p flywheel collab
```
close_reason: fix-root-causes — the lost reply was a baseline captured too late, not a timing flake, so the baseline now comes from the ask's own id instead of a re-read of the thread head. Reading further down the same path found the un-scoped read truncated to the OLDEST rows, which would have kept the wait failing after the baseline fix alone.

title: fix: flywheel mail inbox fails — orchestrator identity not registered in target project
description:
BUG (real-world): `flywheel mail inbox ` fails with: Agent 'CoralFinch' not found. Project '' has no registered agents yet. Use register_agent to create an agent identity first ... when the configured flywheel mail identity (e.g. CoralFinch) is not registered in the target project. ## Root cause `MailCmd::Inbox` (src/main.rs:3298) calls `ensure_project` then `mail.inbox(&key, &name, ...)` where `name = mail.name` (the configured identity, e.g. CoralFinch). The agent-mail `fetch_inbox` MCP tool requires the agent to be **registered in that project**. The inbox command calls `ensure_project` but NEVER `register_agent`. `cmd_spawn` registers *spawned agents*, and registers them only in the project they were spawned into. The orchestrator identity (mail.name) is never self-registered, so any project the orchestrator never spawned into (or where the identity wasn't registered by some other path) has no row for it -> `fetch_inbox` rejects. The same defect affects `MailProductCmd::Inbox` (src/main.rs:3420, product-scoped inbox). ## Fix `MailCmd::Inbox` and `MailProductCmd::Inbox` must idempotently self-register the orchestrator identity before fetching. `register_agent` is an upsert (idempotent on name — re-register updates profile + refreshes last_active_ts), so this is safe to call every inbox. Register with program/model = "flywheel" and a descriptive task like "flywheel orchestrator". This mirrors what `cmd_spawn` does for spawned agents (src/main.rs:1733). The orchestrator needs the same treatment for its own inbox. ## Acceptance - `flywheel mail inbox ` works (exit 0, returns inbox JSON or empty array) — the identity is registered as a side effect. - `flywheel mail inbox flywheel` still works (idempotent re-register on an already-registered identity). - `flywheel mail product inbox --product

` works for fresh products. - The registered identity appears in `flywheel mail agents ` after inbox. - Test covers: inbox registers-then-fetches (mock or assertion on register_agent call ordering). ## Notes - Do NOT change the error when the mail backend itself is unconfigured (`mail_or_die` already bails correctly). - `register_agent` failure should warn to stderr but NOT abort the inbox fetch (best-effort self-register — the fetch may still fail with a clear server error, which is the honest signal).
close_reason: Fixed: MailCmd::Inbox idempotently self-registers orchestrator identity before fetch_inbox. register_agent is an upsert, safe every call. Failure is non-fatal (warn to stderr).

principles.name: a-silent-empty-success-is-worse-than-a-failure
principles.decision: 87 percent of dispatches returned nothing while reporting success, and no caller can tell that from working

principles.name: never-rewrite-the-measurement
principles.decision: the 383 empty run records ARE the evidence

title: headless dispatch returns an EMPTY response with status=success — 383 of 442 run records, so every workflow that dispatches a job gets a silent no-op
description:
FOUND BY RUNNING A WORKFLOW LIVE, 2026-09-29. No test covers this and no health field names it.
It is the single largest coordination defect found this session, and it is invisible from the
outside because every affected run reports SUCCESS.

THE MEASUREMENT. 442 headless (`hl-`) run records in ~/.local/state/flywheel/runs. 383 of them
(87%) have an EMPTY `response` while carrying real wall time, `exit_code: 0` and
`status: "success"`. Only 59 produced any text at all. The one I triggered by hand:

    run_id  hl-2026-09-28T17:08:09Z-780903000
    workflow awareness-digest   profile housekeeper   harness opencode
    mode headless   prompt_hash 18d5be86…   duration_ms 126242   exit_code 0
    response ""      tokens_in 0      tokens_out 0      status success

Two minutes of wall time, a real prompt hash, exit 0, and nothing came back.

THE MECHANISM, in `parse_stream` (crates/../src/headless.rs:239-312). Three lines decide everything:

    let Ok(v) = serde_json::from_str::<Value>(line) else { continue; };   // 253
    saw_json = true;                                                     // 255
    …
    if !saw_json { response = stdout.to_string(); }                       // 296

`saw_json` is set by ANY parseable JSON line, and then SUPPRESSES the raw-stdout fallback. The
response is otherwise only ever assigned from a line that is simultaneously `type ==
"message_end"`, `role == "assistant"`, and carries non-empty `content[].text` (257-280). And
`status` is `"success"` unless `error` was set, which can only happen INSIDE a `message_end`
(263-270).

So a harness that emits one parseable JSON line — a banner, a status frame, a different vendor
shape — and then delivers its answer as anything other than that exact triple produces:

    response ""   tokens 0/0   status success   exit_code 0

Non-JSON lines are not merely unused as a fallback; they are DISCARDED at 253 under the comment
"banner noise, not stream corruption". For a harness whose answer arrives as plain text after a JSON
header, the answer IS the discarded content.

THE THREE MISSING BRANCHES. Each is a state the function can reach and silently reports as success:

  1. `saw_json` and no `message_end` line at all -> the stream shape is unrecognised. That is a
     FAILURE to agree on a protocol and should say so.
  2. `message_end` seen, no assistant text -> the agent finished without answering. Also not success.
  3. The skipped non-JSON lines should be retained and used as a LAST-RESORT response when no
     assistant message was found, which is strictly better than returning "" while claiming success.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A COSMETIC PARSE BUG. A workflow whose step consumes a dispatched
response cannot tell "the agent worked and said nothing" from "the response was never captured",
because both are `success` with an empty string. Any gate, branch or artifact built on that response
is reading nothing and cannot know it. The whole dispatch half of the workflow engine is therefore
unverified in practice: the 87% figure is not 87% of dispatches failing loudly, it is 87% of them
failing SILENTLY, and the remaining 13% is the only evidence anyone has that the path works at all.

WHAT I DID NOT DO. I did not "fix" it by loosening the success condition or by defaulting the
response to raw stdout unconditionally — both would make the number look better while destroying the
distinction between a real answer and a parse miss. I also did not change any recorded historical
run; the 383 empty records are the evidence and rewriting them would be falsifying the measurement.

THE MINIMAL HONEST FIX, for whoever owns headless.rs: make the three states above DISTINGUISHABLE.
`saw_json` with no usable assistant message must be a failure that NAMES what it saw, because
"unrecognised stream shape" and "agent said nothing" and "the harness answered in a shape this build
does not know" are three different bugs and today they are one indistinguishable success.

WORTH PAIRING WITH A LIVE FIXTURE. A recorded stdout sample from the `opencode` harness, asserted
through `parse_stream`, would have caught this at the unit level. The absence of one is why 442 runs
could be uninformative for a long time without a single red test.
close_reason: Fixed and committed at 4bb448f. The parser was silent on the one line that mattered: parse_stream read an error only from INSIDE a type:"message_end" frame, and set saw_json on any parseable JSON line, which SUPPRESSES the raw-stdout fallback. A harness reporting a failure any other way produced response:"", status:"success", and no error at all. Only 29 of 383 empty runs carry an error field; 354 are success with an empty response and NO diagnostic. Also fixed a second real defect the analysis surfaced: stderr was THE error whenever the response was empty, so a NO_COLOR warning was logged 20 times as the reason a dispatch produced nothing, and it overwrote real parse errors. NOT DONE: the 72 long runs are not yet diagnosed - they need a recorded stdout fixture per harness, sliced on duration. I did not rewrite the 383 historical records; they are the evidence. RETRACTION recorded on the bead: my first root cause (context-length overflow) was inferred from one manual run that never entered the run log, and three measurements refute it.

comments.author: bangedorrunt
comments.text:
BREAKDOWN BY HARNESS, which turns the 87% aggregate into something specific and actionable. Grouped over all 442 hl- records:

    harness   profile        runs  empty    pct
    opencode  coder            65     65   100%
    opencode  reviewer         53     53   100%
    opencode  scout            37     37   100%
    opencode  planner          15     15   100%
    opencode  housekeeper       1      1   100%
    opencode  verify-*          6      6   100%   (verify-cond x4, verify-preamble, and one more)
    pi        planner          76     63    83%
    omp       oracle           34     26    76%
    pi        coder            14     13    93%
    omp       coder            19     14    74%
    omp       planner          25     12    48%
    pi        reviewer         11     11   100%
    omp       housekeeper       9      9   100%
    omp       reviewer          8      8   100%
    omp       scout            16      4    25%
    pi        oracle            2      0     0%   <-- the path CAN work
    pi        housekeeper       3      0     0%   <-- and again
    omp       verify-rm-live    1      0     0%

THE HEADLINE IS NOT '87 PERCENT'. IT IS THAT THE opencode PATH HAS NEVER WORKED. Every single opencode run — all seven profiles, 177 records — is empty, with zero exceptions. That is not a flaky parse; it is a shape mismatch that is total and permanent for the dominant harness on this host.

And the pi/oracle, pi/housekeeper and omp/verify-rm-live rows are the CONTROL: the same code path, the same profile machinery, zero empty responses. So parse_stream is not universally broken — it agrees with SOME harness output and never with opencode's. That is exactly the 'saw_json is set by any parseable JSON line, then suppresses the raw-stdout fallback' diagnosis: a harness that emits a JSON line and its answer in any other shape loses the answer every time, while a harness whose answer is plain text with no JSON survives on the fallback.

So the fix is not 'be more tolerant in general'. It is: find out what opencode actually emits on a headless dispatch and either parse that shape or stop discarding the non-JSON lines. The 100%/0% split is strong enough to make this a one-harness investigation rather than a redesign, and it is falsifiable — one recorded opencode stdout sample settles it, which is why I asked for a live fixture in the bead body.

Worth noting for whoever picks it up: the 6 opencode verify-* records at 100% are the ones that would have been most valuable. A verification step that reports success with an empty response is worse than no verification step, because the workflow believes the check ran.

comments.author: bangedorrunt
comments.text:
RETRACTION of the root cause I first recorded, and it is wrong. I inferred it from one manual invocation that never entered the run log.

WHAT I CLAIMED: that the 87% empty is a context-length overflow, because I ran `opencode run --format json 'reply with exactly: PONG'` by hand, got `maximum context length is 36864 tokens … you requested about 37930`, and generalised.

WHY IT WAS WRONG, in three measurements.

1. NO RECORDED RUN HAS THAT ERROR. Of the 383 empty run records, the recorded error strings are: 20x `Warning: The 'NO_COLOR' env is ignored…`, 11x `harness exited exit status: 1`, 10x a 402 credit/`max_tokens` refusal, 3x `Model "@premium" not found`, 3x an internal API error. ZERO context-length errors. The thing I generalised from is not in the data at all — it was a single run I performed myself, from /tmp, with a 4-word prompt, and it was never written to the run log.

2. THE DURATION DISTRIBUTION REFUTES IT DIRECTLY. A context rejection is an instant HTTP 400 with no generation, so every such run must be sub-second. But of the 383 empty runs: 263 are <1s, 48 are 1-10s, 49 are 10-60s and 23 are >=60s. So 72 empty runs lasted 10s or more, several at 322s-531s — 5 to 9 minutes of wall time. Those cannot be rejections; something ran for nine minutes and returned nothing. My own awareness-digest run was 126s, squarely in that population, and I used it as if it supported the claim when it actually contradicts it.

3. THE POPULATION IS HETEROGENEOUS, so a single cause was never plausible. 87% was never one thing.

WHAT THE SAME ANALYSIS DID FIND, which is real and worth more than the wrong claim.

Only 29 of the 383 empty runs carry an `error` field at all. 354 are recorded as a SUCCESS with an empty response and NO diagnostic of any kind — so for 92% of the empty population there is nothing to diagnose even in principle.

And one recorded "error" is a FALSE ATTRIBUTION, which is a defect in its own right: main.rs:29867 does `if outcome.response.is_empty() && !stderr.trim().is_empty() { outcome.error = Some(stderr) }`. So ANY stderr line becomes THE error whenever the response is empty. A `NO_COLOR` warning is recorded 20 times as the reason a run produced nothing, which is the least informative possible answer and it displaces the real cause. Worse, this also OVERWRITES the parse error that the bd-7wah fix now produces, so the genuine provider message can be clobbered by a warning printed after it.

The 3x `Model "@premium" not found` are the same defect as bd-ziy9 (the slot ladder failing on a real run rather than in a test), which is independent corroboration that the profile/harness work is hitting production.

WHAT STANDS from my original report: the parser fix. A top-level `type: "error"` was never read, an unrecognised stream shape was reported as success, and the 72 long empty runs are exactly the population that fix addresses. What does NOT stand is the context-length explanation, and the honest next step is to find what the 72 long runs actually emitted — which needs a recorded stdout fixture per harness, the same ask as before, now with the duration split as the thing to slice on.

title: Packer folds a role onto another pane but pane_dispatch still resolves the @role exactly, so the run bails
description:
Distinct from the spawn/list race in bd-ietv, and live-confirmed on 2026-09-27 with the bd-ietv fix installed. The goal workflow (src/builtin_workflows.rs:304-341) needs FIVE unique roles: its ideate step calls ce-brainstorm, which dispatches @oracle and @planner; build is @coder, review is @reviewer, ship is @housekeeper. 'crew: auto' packs unique roles into N panes and, when N is below the unique count, FOLDS the remainder onto existing panes. The pack log says it outright: 'packing goal into 3 panes (cap=5, unique=5): coder, planner, reviewer (housekeeper -> coder, oracle -> coder)'. pane_dispatch resolves a step's @role only by exact profile match or exact name match (resolve_pane_entry, src/pane.rs:152-171) and bails when neither hits. It does NOT know about the fold. So a folded @oracle has no row, settle_role_with correctly declines it (no row means never spawned, per its own contract), and the step fails: 'pane dispatch: no crew pane for @oracle (spawned: EmberOtter, coder, planner, reviewer)'. Live evidence at --crew 3 with bd-ietv installed: the run's final pane list held exactly four entries (EmberOtter, crew-goal-coder, crew-goal-planner, crew-goal-reviewer) — no oracle and no housekeeper pane was ever created — and all three dispatch_job steps still failed on @oracle. So there are two separate faults behind the same error string: a prune race that drops a row that EXISTS (bd-ietv, needs N >= unique so nothing folds), and this fold, where the row never existed. Fixing one does not fix the other. Fix: make dispatch honour the fold the packer already decided. Either record the alias on the spawned row so resolve_pane_entry can match a folded role, or expose the packer's role->pane map to the dispatcher and resolve through it. A fold that the dispatcher cannot see is a fold that breaks the run, so the two must agree by construction rather than by convention. Acceptance: 'flywheel steer --project

--crew 3' completes the goal workflow; a test proves a role the packer folded onto another pane dispatches to that pane, and that a role with neither a row nor a fold still bails loud.
close_reason: status: fixed; commit 4d445e3505590de4332692ec1be8144c84d66e87; gate unit-test-verified=pass, ledger check LEGAL at that sha. ROOT CAUSE: the fold was decided in ONE place and applied in another that could not see it. apply_role_aliases (already in HEAD) rewrites the document it is handed, so a folded @role lands only when the PARENT dispatches that role. goal dispatches coder/housekeeper/reviewer and gets its @oracle from ce-brainstorm via call_workflow, so at --crew 3 the packer folds oracle->coder and announces it, the parent rewrite changes nothing, and the child keeps asking for a pane that was never spawned: the original bd-8c5h bail, one indirection deeper than the fix that already existed. FIX: aliasing_resolver wraps the base resolver and applies the SAME apply_role_aliases to every child, so the rewrite logic keeps one home and the fold travels one document deeper rather than being reimplemented. A child the base cannot resolve stays unresolvable (inventing an empty document would let a missing sub-workflow run and report success); an empty alias map returns the base resolver untouched, so a crew that fits its budget is byte-identical to the previous path. Wired into BOTH sub-run resolvers (workflow run and compose --run) because a fold reaching only one is the same defect a level down. EVIDENCE: the_fold_reaches_the_child_that_dispatches_the_role runs against the REAL builtins, not a fixture, and asserts goal dispatches roles but NOT @oracle, ce-brainstorm DOES dispatch @oracle, and the existing parent rewrite is a no-op for a role the parent never dispatches; if either builtin changes shape the preconditions fail instead of the test asserting nothing. That precondition caught a wrong premise in my first draft, written from 'workflow show' summary output which does not print dispatch profiles. Falsified by neutering the wrapper to return the child untouched: fails with 'the fold never reached the child document: ["oracle", "planner", "reviewer"]' — @oracle surviving unfurled, the production bail verbatim. Two more tests pin the no-fold identity and that an unresolvable child is not manufactured. FENCE HONESTY: the bead's own verify 'test -p flywheel pane_dispatch' runs 2 tests and passes but does not reach this code, so it was measured and the whole workspace run instead: 1974+161+70 passed, 0 failed. fmt and clippy clean in the files touched; the pre-existing doorbell-rt unused import and three pre-existing fmt diffs are not mine and were left alone. SCOPE DISCIPLINE: another agent was landing bd-07m2 in src/pane.rs concurrently; I committed ONLY src/crew.rs and src/main.rs and verified no foreign content was staged. NOT DONE, stated rather than hidden: no live 'steer --crew 3' goal run — that path's ship step is commit-and-push against a real repo, an operator authorisation, not an agent's to take. The unit fence proves the fold reaches the child document; it does not prove a real crew completes. PRINCIPLES: fix-root-causes - the fold was decided in the packer and applied in a rewriter that could not see a call_workflow child, so the fix makes the decision travel with the resolver instead of teaching the dispatcher a second way to learn about folds. prove-it-works - the bead's own fence matched tests that never reach the changed code, so the fence was measured (2 tests) and the whole workspace run instead of reporting a narrow green as proof.

comments.author: bangedorrunt
comments.text:
PeachRobin claimed 10:35Z, read the root cause, wrote a RED test, then stood down: another agent is ALREADY implementing bd-8c5h concurrently and has the tree RED. Releasing the claim so the real implementer is not blocked. No files of mine remain modified.

ROOT CAUSE: apply_role_aliases (src/crew.rs:557) rewrites only the document it is handed. A call_workflow child is a DIFFERENT document reached through the injected WorkflowResolver, so a fold of a child-owned role never reaches the child. goal step 1 is call_workflow ce-brainstorm, and ce-brainstorm dispatches @oracle - a role the packer folds onto coder at --crew 3. The child still spells @oracle, pane_dispatch finds no pane, run bails under a green pack log.

IN FLIGHT: option (a) - a folded_roles field on state::SpawnEntry, matched at pane.rs:257 and :335, set at spawn at pane.rs:1018. I deliberately did NOT also implement option (b) (wrapping the resolver in crew.rs). Two competing designs; only one should ship.

TREE IS RED, 8 errors, all from that in-flight change: 4x E0063 missing field folded_roles in SpawnEntry fixtures (pane.rs:2636+), 2x E0609 no field folded on CrewPlan (main.rs references a field that does not exist yet). flywheel does not compile, so no agent can verify anything until it lands.

VERIFIED FACT worth keeping: ce-brainstorm does NOT fan out @oracle x3. It is a graph with three separate nodes (diverge_oracle, diverge_structure, diverge_risk), each dispatching one role once, with no over:. The module doc at builtin_workflows.rs:10 and the doc at pane.rs:293 both still claim over: 3 - both stale. So oracle needs exactly 1 pane and the fold IS legitimate.

title: doorbell autohost is unimplemented: nothing reads Subscription.project, so no wake is ever routed
description:
Autohost does not exist, so the entire wake contract is a flywheel-side promise with no consumer. This is why doorbell never woke me, and it is a much bigger finding than "the host was not armed".

THE EVIDENCE, all verified against the current trees.

1. flywheel writes the rows and promises a consumer. src/doorbell.rs:456 (bd-kj2z) register_arrival_subscription says "the daemon auto-hosts the named pair within 60s" and stamps project: Some(project) on the row. src/cmd/doorbell.rs:542 REFUSES a project-less subscribe with the justification "a project-less row is never auto-hosted, so the wake would never ring. Pass --project <slug>." So a whole refusal path exists to protect a mechanism that does not exist.

2. Nothing in toron implements it. grep -rniE 'autohost|auto_host|auto-host|bd-2o1v' over the whole toron tree (excluding target) returns exactly ONE hit: a mention of bd-2o1v in docs/decisions/0032-workflow-engine-honesty-jido-contracts.md, and that is about workflow effect journaling, not autohosting. There is no autohost code, no autohost field, no autohost loop.

3. The field has no reader. grep for '.project' across toron/crates returns only binds on workflow_effects rows — a different type. NOTHING reads Subscription.project. flywheel writes it on every arrive and every subscribe --project, and no code in any crate consumes it.

So: every arrival row and every project-scoped subscription is currently dead weight, and no wake is ever routed by project. The daemon's /health `hosted` list is populated some other way (it does contain flywheel/flywheel-flywheel, the label scope arrive writes to), but nothing ADDS a host because a row appeared.

WHY IT LOOKED LIKE "just needs arming". The status line says "does not host flywheel/adrx2728 — arm it: doorbell start --host flywheel/adrx2728", which reads like a missing flag. It is not: that flag would host a scope by hand, and the next arrive would still not be honoured, because the row-to-host path does not exist. A second, independent mismatch compounds it — arrive scopes the row to swarm_label(project) ("flywheel-flywheel") while the live session scope is the herdr workspace id (adrx2728), so even a working autohost would have to reconcile label against id.

WHAT A FIX REQUIRES (toron side, so it needs an owner there — flywheel cannot fix it alone).
- Something must read Subscription.project and ensure the daemon hosts that (project, scope) pair within a bounded time. That is the whole missing consumer.
- Decide whether the scope is a herdr workspace ID or a project label. flywheel writes the label; the daemon's hosted list contains labels; but per-workspace leases and `watch_idle` are keyed by workspace id. Both bd-ene2 (leases per workspace) and bd-2o1v (autohost) depend on that answer, so resolve it once and reuse it.
- A subscribe row must be able to ADD a host to a running daemon, and a dead row must be able to REMOVE one. Today the only way to change `hosted` is a restart with --host flags, which is why the set looks static.
- Bounded work: do not re-scan every row on every tick forever. The arrival reaper already exists ("stale pins age out via the daemon reaper"), so autohost should hang off the same reconcile rather than a second poller.

VERIFY by arming nothing by hand: create a fresh subscription in a scratch project, then assert within the documented window that the daemon's /health `hosted` list GAINS the scope without any restart and without a --host flag. Then assert a removed/aged row drops it. A manual `doorbell start --host` proves nothing, because that path already works.

ALSO NOTE, because it is the same class of bug and already fixed on our side: bd-2zqk (2a76588) was flywheel's health probe reporting a healthy daemon as "unreachable" 33% of the time, which sent the operator to start a daemon that was already running. Diagnosing this one was made harder by that. The general lesson: a degraded-mode warning must name the condition it actually observed, not a plausible-sounding one.
close_reason: bd-8kn9 CLOSED AS RETRACTED (operator-directed gate, deliberately not unit-test-verified because a retracted research claim has no test). Autohost is implemented and working: crates/doorbell-cli/src/serve.rs:829-850 runs a 60s reconcile whose reconcile_once lists subscriptions, computes unhosted_subscribed, takes a lease, prints auto-hosting {project}/{workspace} (subscribed) and calls spawn_host_loop - documented at :939 as shared by boot-time --host config and dynamic auto-host, and idempotent so the two cannot double-ring. My error was searching toron for a doorbell that lives in flywheel own workspace, inferring ownership from the binary name instead of the build graph; the proof was already in my context because the daemon hosted flywheel/flywheel-flywheel, a pair never passed via --host, and after a restart it re-populated all 11 pairs by itself. The REAL cause is bd-lmtu: the daemon leaked threads until it held 4464 of a 6000 ulimit -u budget, could not spawn its watch threads, and crash-looped its watch/reconcile loops, which is exactly what degraded:[watch_restart_loop] reported throughout. Still open: the arrival subscription is scoped to swarm_label(project) while the live session scope is the herdr workspace id that is therefore never subscribed; bd-ene2 per-workspace leases need the same label-vs-id answer, so settle it once and reuse it.

comments.author: bangedorrunt
comments.text:
RETRACTION. The claim in this bead that autohost is unimplemented is WRONG, and the error was looking in the wrong repository.

What I searched: grep for autohost/auto_host/auto-host across toron. What I should have searched first: the doorbell crates are NOT in toron. They are flywheel own workspace members - Cargo.toml lists crates/doorbell-core, crates/doorbell-rt, crates/doorbell-cli. doorbell serve is built from crates/doorbell-cli/src/serve.rs.

Autohost is implemented and running. crates/doorbell-cli/src/serve.rs:829-850 spawns a reconcile task that calls reconcile_once every 60s. reconcile_once (serve.rs ~1089-1128) does exactly what this bead said was missing: it lists subscriptions, computes unhosted_subscribed(subs, hosted_keys(hosted)), takes a lease per pair, prints "auto-hosting {project}/{workspace} (subscribed)", and calls spawn_host_loop - which serve.rs:939 documents as "shared by boot-time --host config and dynamic auto-host" and which is idempotent so boot config and reconcile cannot double-ring one workspace. It then calls retire_unsubscribed (bd-mk60) to drop hosts whose subscriptions went away. So a subscription row DOES add a host to a running daemon, and a dead row DOES remove one. Both halves this bead called impossible exist.

Confirmed live, which is what should have stopped me: the daemon /health hosted list contains flywheel/flywheel-flywheel, and that pair was never passed via --host. It got there by autohost. I read that very list earlier in this session as evidence and did not connect it.

title: The tear signal is one boolean: it cannot say how big, where, or how much history it hid, so a designed retention drop is indistinguishable from a lost write
description:
journal_torn_tail is reported as a bare kind name, and fold_workspace STOPS at the first tear, so everything after it is unreachable from 'doorbell why'. Two live examples that read identically: opencode, 16 seqs missing (153411-153426, one lost append, 771 rows withheld from the fold); chiebukuro, 89 gaps in 4,939 rows including one jump of 5,175 seqs.

Worse, a drop the daemon performs itself was reported as a tear. rotate() already records journal_rotated with dropped_lines/dropped_bytes in the audit sidecar (my earlier report that 'no rotation row exists' was wrong — I had grepped the journal instead of the audit sidecar), but the record carried no link to the seq stream, so the fold could not tell retention from corruption and seven workspaces sat permanently degraded for drops the daemon made on purpose.

Fix: TornTail carries missing_seqs, missing_from, missing_to and rows_withheld, and the LoudMiss row carries all of them. rotate() records the seq range it removes (read before deleting, never guessed — a drop with no range is recorded as null so it cannot excuse a real loss). RetentionDrop::explains classifies a gap covered by a record as retention: not a tear, and the fold continues past it instead of discarding the readable tail. remaining: journal() still advances next_seq BEFORE the append and discards the append error, so a failed write still burns a seq silently (tracked in bd-5qyt).

title: wake: an unrecorded harness kind must still be injectable
description:
Follow-up to bd-harness-caps-6r1x, found by checking the live registries against the new table.

The commit made an unknown kind a NoDoor: wake_route returned NoDoor(Mail) for any kind with no row, so ring_wake typed nothing and the inbox ring failed. The live state does not support that: 46 of the 53 entries in ~/.local/state/flywheel/agents/*.json carry NO harness field (legacy rows, kind = ""), and pane_write::Harness::from_kind already knows claude/claude-code/cc and codex/cx, which have no row either. Those panes are herdr panes: the sink types into them today, and the harness kind only picks the launch bootstrap (launch_bootstrap returns one PULL contract for every variant). So unknown-knid-refuses is a regression against working wakes, not conservatism.

Fix:
- Add the full kind vocabulary the repo already maps (claude/cc/claude-code, codex/cx) to the table, with the same inject/interrupt/resume witnesses as the other pane rows.
- Split the policy: route_for(row, kind, hook_installed) answers for a row, wake_route(kind, installed) = route_for(row(kind), ...). An unrecorded kind (None row, empty field, or a kind nobody mapped) routes Inject { interrupt: true }: the pane is herdr-managed and the sink types into it. NoDoor stays reachable for a recorded row that refuses injection, which is the shape a future non-pokeable harness takes.
- Rewrite wake_falls_back_when_harness_cannot_inject to drive BOTH branches: a synthetic refusing row gets NoDoor with the mail fallback and the sink types nothing; an unrecorded kind still injects. The send door keeps its note path for a refusing row.

Risk if unfixed: every legacy pin and every claude/codex pane goes dark for wake mail.
