title: CI has not executed since 2026-09-25: GitHub Actions is billing-blocked, so every run is a 2-5s non-start that looks like a test failure
description:
The independent verification gate is dark, and its failure mode imitates a real one.

Evidence (gh run list, 2026-09-28): the last five pushes to main each report conclusion=failure, and every one of them failed in 2-5 SECONDS across all six jobs. `gh run view 36312213062` gives the actual annotation:

    X The job was not started because recent account payments have failed or
      your spending limit needs to be increased. Please check the 'Billing &
      plans' section in your settings

So no job ran; no test, check, clippy or fmt step was reached. Six jobs at 2-5s is the tell — a job that ran and failed would be minutes long (the bin suite is sharded precisely because it is slow).

Why this matters more than a normal outage:
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` exists because 'flywheel had no Actions; every local \"suite green\" claim was unverifiable remotely' (its own header, GS-018). That property is currently false: main is unverifiable remotely, and has been for three days while work landed on it.
- The failure LOOKS like a red suite. Anyone reading the checks sees failure x6, which is indistinguishable at a glance from six failing jobs, and the natural next move is to go hunting for a broken test instead of a billing page. Both a false-alarm hunt and a missed real regression are on the table.
- This is exactly the class this repo keeps removing elsewhere: a signal whose state does not mean what it appears to mean (the RestartWatch metric, journal_torn_tail before bd-9ase, the dead clippy gate cleaned in bd-iyq5 — which would have failed this same step the moment billing is restored).

Operator action, not a code change: restore billing/spending limit on the org, then confirm a push actually runs. Nothing in the repo can fix it, and no agent can verify it. Recorded here so the next agent who sees six red checks on main does not go looking for a broken test.

Found while closing bd-iyq5 (the clippy-debt bead): I had written 'the CI lint job is red on main' and then found that it is red for a reason I had not imagined.
close_reason: Operator-waived close: a PRIVATE repo draws on metered Actions minutes and the account is over its allowance, so every job is refused at start. No workflow change can fix it. Evidence recorded; local gates (verify-clippy exit 0, 2084 bin tests) stand in.

principles.decision: a test that passes alone and fails in the suite is an isolation bug, not a flaky test; fix the shared state, never the assertion

title: artifact::tests stitch tests are order-dependent, not isolated
description:
Found while landing bd-crlx. artifact::tests::stitch_reports_a_terminal_only_run_instead_of_a_serde_error and stitch_keeps_typed_records_alongside_a_terminal_outcome both resolve their fixture root via dirs::data_local_dir(), which reads XDG_DATA_HOME / HOME at call time. Other tests in the same binary mutate those vars (via set_var under lock_env()). Running the full bin suite, both artifact tests FAILED; running either alone, or running them on a clean tree, they PASS. So they are not broken by any logic change — they are a latent test-isolation race whose probability shifts whenever the test count or schedule changes. bd-crlx adding 13 tests was enough to surface it.

Fix direction: do not weaken the assertions. Either have these two tests pin the data dir themselves (set XDG_DATA_HOME to a TempDir under the same env lock the mutating tests use) so they cannot observe another test's value, or give them an injected fixture root instead of going through dirs::data_local_dir(). Confirm by running the full suite repeatedly after the fix — a single green run does not prove a race is gone.

Also worth folding in: model_args falls through '_ => vec![] for the claude and codex harnesses, so those pin NO model at all today (pre-existing, found during bd-crlx, deliberately not changed there because it is a behaviour change on a path nobody asked about). Worth a decision: either those harnesses take a model flag or flywheel should refuse to pretend it pinned one.
close_reason: bd-ww75 closed. The two stitch tests were order-dependent, not flaky: both resolved their fixture root through dirs::data_local_dir() at call time while other tests in the same binary mutate XDG_DATA_HOME, so a read could land under a different root than the fixture was written to. Fixed by injection - stitch_artifacts_in plus a per-test xdg_root TempDir - because src/artifact.rs is #![forbid(unsafe_code)] and cannot pin the env at all, which is itself the signal that injection is the right fix. Public signature unchanged so main.rs needed no edit. read_evaluation_evidence deliberately left on the ambient root: parameterizing it broke an unrelated test by duplicating a path builder, and no test was weakened to make anything pass. Evidence in the gate row. The commit this rides is the follow-up that moved xdg_root into the tests module; the FIRST fix commit did not compile and that is recorded in the bead.

comments.author: bangedorrunt
comments.text:
SCOPE CORRECTED by operator decision: the claude/codex part of this bead is NOT a defect, so drop it.

Operator ruling: codex, claude, and grok are frontier proprietary harnesses that flywheel runs on THEIR default model. Model routing for them is intentionally absent, so headless::model_args falling through to '_ => vec![] for those harnesses is the desired policy, not an oversight. Do not 'fix' it, and do not add a model flag for them. The comment I wrote earlier suggesting we 'should refuse to pretend it pinned one' is wrong for these three — running their default IS the intent.

That leaves exactly one live concern in this bead, the actual bug: artifact::tests::stitch_reports_a_terminal_only_run_instead_of_a_serde_error and stitch_keeps_typed_records_alongside_a_terminal_outcome resolve their fixture root through dirs::data_local_dir(), which reads XDG_DATA_HOME/HOME at call time, while other tests in the same binary mutate those vars. They pass alone and on a clean tree but failed in a full suite run. Fix the shared state (pin the data dir to a TempDir under the same env lock, or inject the fixture root); do not weaken the assertions, and do not treat one green full-suite run as proof the race is gone.

Also recorded as policy, not a defect: model routing is OPTIONAL. Where a harness has a sane default (opencode, pi), running on its default model is a legitimate choice, so any future routing work must be additive and never mandatory.

This one is the opposite: a gate that is RED while its subject has moved on. Either the brain wake-save path stopped warning with arm context (a real honesty regression in the doorbell), or the tripwire is asserting a string that was renamed and nobody updated the assertion. title: flywheel has no stale-build check: the tier-aware harness menu was invisible for 16.5h behind a stale installed binary
description:
The tier-aware harness menu has been INVISIBLE to an operator for 16.5 hours,
because flywheel has no staleness check for its own installed binary.

NOT A CODE BUG. Measured 2026-09-28 with a temporary probe in cmd_briefing:

  PROBE: catalog OK, 9 profiles
  PROBE: harness_menu present = true

The menu builds correctly and `flywheel briefing --json` emits it. The INSTALLED
binary was from 2026-09-27T12:32:47Z and predates the wiring, so the field was
absent from every briefing for 16.5h while looking like a missing feature. Fixed by
installing the current build; the menu now renders on `flywheel briefing` and the
live output is:

  crew: 3
    opencode | tier open | roles [coder, reviewer] | slot cheap
    pi       | tier open | roles [planner]       | slot standard
  registered_unconfigured: [omp, pa, jcode, grok, codex, claude, fx]

THE GAP. The doorbell grew a `stale_build` degradation this session (bd-v7uu): it
compares SOURCE against the running exe, because wall-clock AGE is a proxy that
cries wolf on a healthy daemon. flywheel — the ORCHESTRATOR, the binary every other
gate depends on — has no equivalent. The symptom is identical and just as expensive:
a feature that appears missing when it is actually deployed-but-stale.

Two costs, and the second is worse than the first. The first is the 16.5h of missing
output. The second is DIAGNOSIS: I spent this round auditing the code, proving the
wiring correct at briefing.rs:81 and the load at main.rs:13302, and only found it by
noticing the installed binary's mtime. Nothing in the product said "you are running
yesterday's build" — a `flywheel --version` that reports the BUILD's mtime next to
the version, or a warn when the exe is older than the newest source, would have made
it a 5-second check.

Also worth recording because it has now happened to me THREE times tonight: I ran
`flywheel` from PATH and concluded a feature was missing, when `target/debug/flywheel`
had it. Testing the installed binary instead of a fresh build nearly produced a false
"not implemented" conclusion, exactly as it nearly produced a false "proven" earlier.
The rule is the same in both directions: verify against the artifact you are shipping.

STILL UNEXERCISED, and it is not a code gap: only `opencode` and `pi` have profiles
on this host, so a crew of 3 has exactly 2 options and `enforce_diversity_floor`
returns early (`options.len() <= floor`). The diversity rule has never fired against
a real catalog. Exercising it needs a third configured profile — `codex` is already
registered and tiered closed, and appears under registered_unconfigured, so adding a
profile for it is the cheapest way to make the rule real. That is an operator choice
about which model this host is allowed to reach.

comments.text:
== round 2: root causes confirmed, fixed, installed, live-verified ==

Root causes beyond round 1 (from code + log + launchd state):
1. serve ran its drain INSIDE tokio::select! while the tcp/uds listeners stayed bound -> probes were accepted but never answered -> misread as "non-doorbell squatter" (80 log lines).
2. stop booted out launchd BEFORE signalling: launchd SIGKILLs at its 5s exit timeout (beheading the drain), and STOP_GRACE was 5s vs an unbounded drain -> false "pid ignored SIGTERM or endpoint stayed live within 5s".
3. start forgot the child handle and polled /health only -> a child that died at the bind fence was reported 15s later as "never answered /health" (pid 68346); the real cause existed only in the log.
4. The squatter bail exited 1 -> KeepAlive{SuccessfulExit=false} respawn-war (launchctl runs=69, health degraded watch_restart_loop).
5. stop never re-armed supervision: restart ended as a raw child with the unit unloaded -> no autostart after reboot.

Fixes (crates/doorbell-cli/src/lifecycle.rs, serve.rs, main.rs; operator permission on record):
- serve: drop listeners FIRST on SIGTERM, bounded DRAIN_BUDGET=10s (loud timeout), classify_port_holder Peer/Unresponsive/Foreign, every AddrInUse conflict exits 0 (stay dead, per lifecycle.rs header).
- stop: TERM -> STOP_GRACE=15s -> SIGKILL -> KILL_GRACE=5s; endpoint survivor after pid death = foreign-holder error naming lsof; stop_target falls back to the live /health owner pid (pidfile-less stop works); disable_supervisor guarded by unit_body_serves so scratch/temp-dir stops never unload THE unit; summary reports escalation.
- start: waits out a busy-unresponsive port; byte-identical installed unit -> supervised bootstrap/kickstart (restart ends supervised); child watched via try_wait, failures report exit status + 4KB log tail via start_failure_brief; reap escalates to SIGKILL and waits only its own pid.
- main: "migrated 0 file(s)" prints only when files actually moved (the empty legacy dir re-printed it on every command).

Verification:

principles.name: fix-root-causes
principles.decision: the file that deletes rows is the one that must not discard its own write errors

title: rotation discards every write error and then reports a clean drop, so a failed rotation loses rows and audits them as designed
description:
The store's own writes are the last place in this subsystem still swallowing failures, and they are the writes that DELETE rows.

crates/doorbell-rt/src/store.rs, rotate():
    let _ = std::fs::rename(&from, self.journal_gen_file(workspace, n + 1));   // 379
    let _ = std::fs::write(self.journal_gen_file(workspace, 1), head...);      // 382
    let _ = std::fs::write(&active, tail.join("\n") + "\n");                   // 383
    let _ = std::fs::write(&p, keep.join("\n") + "\n");                       // 422
and then, unconditionally, one audit row claiming a clean drop with a seq range (427-438). Its own doc says 'Every drop is an audit row' — true about the ROW, false about the drop: if the active rewrite at 383 fails after the read, or the process dies mid-write, the active journal is truncated or partial and the row that follows reports a tidy drop of N lines. That is the chiebukuro shape exactly: four generation files on disk (so rotation ran at least four times), 89 gaps, one 5,175 seqs wide, and the sum of recorded dropped_lines is ZERO. A record that says 'nothing was lost' while rows are gone is worse than no record, because the fold trusts it.

Note what the seq range did and did not fix: bd-9ase made a drop record carry seq_from/seq_to so a designed drop stops reading as a tear. That is only sound while the drop actually HAPPENED. A failed rotation that still records a range would excuse a real gap forever — the failure mode has to land on the SAFE side, i.e. no range, plus the failure, plus a loud line.

Also: append_audit() (736) discards its own write error twice over — `let _ = private_dir(parent)` and `let _ = writeln!(f, ...)` inside an `if let Ok(...)`. So the evidence channel can stop recording in total silence. That is the exact sibling of the journal defect bd-5qyt fixed: same shape, one file over, and it matters more because the journal's tear reports are delivered THROUGH the audit.

FIX: (1) an atomic replace helper (write a temp beside the target, rename over it) for every destructive rewrite, so a failed rotation is a no-op instead of a truncation; (2) collect the failures and, when there are any, keep the row but DROP its seq range (a range is only recordable for rows we are sure we removed) and name the failed step; (3) warn on stderr at the moment of failure; (4) append_audit returns io::Result so a caller that can act may, with the loud line fired inside it either way.
close_reason: done

principles.name: a-fence-in-code-not-a-comment
principles.decision: the structural retention claim is now proven by a test, because the file gate P2b reads had no test at all

principles.name: declining-to-build-is-an-outcome
principles.decision: the measured problem was 16 rows, not 117, and the only available prune would have disarmed the gate it was meant to serve

title: bd-3uqz item D: .unanswered row-retention is DELIBERATELY not built — retention is already structural and the prune would disarm P2b
description:
NOT IMPLEMENTED, ON PURPOSE. This is the bead's item D, closed as a finding rather than as code, and the
reasoning is the deliverable.

THE BEAD ASKED FOR: "prune ROWS older than a retention window (an unanswered pin from three weeks ago
is not going to be answered), never prune a file that still has live rows, and tombstone rather than
delete when a file empties."

THOSE THREE CLAUSES ARE MUTUALLY INCONSISTENT, which is the first sign the design was written without
reading the code. "Never prune a file that still has live rows" means a file can only empty by every
one of its rows ageing out — but the rows are bare pins with NO TIMESTAMP. A row is a line of text
("EmberOtter"). There is nothing to age. So the policy as written is not implementable without first
changing the file format.

THE MEASUREMENT, which is what settled it. Re-surveyed 2026-09-28:

    16 files, 16 ROWS TOTAL. 12 of the 16 files have ZERO rows.

The bead's own survey said the two active files held 66 and 51 rows. Today they hold 6 and 5. The
117-row backlog is not a backlog any more, and there was never a per-row leak to close.

WHY THERE IS NO PER-ROW LEAK. `Hear::heard` and the late-pubkey path both call
`self.unanswered.remove(pin)` (brain.rs:2698, :2726), and `persist_hear()` REWRITES the whole file
from the live set on every sweep (brain.rs:1112, called at :483, :571, :670, :743). So a row exists
if and only if the pin is unanswered RIGHT NOW. A pin unanswered for three weeks is not stale data
awaiting a window: it is re-written every 17 seconds, and if it is absent from the file it has already
been answered. There is nothing for an age policy to reclaim.

SO A PRUNE HERE WOULD DO THE OPPOSITE OF THE BEAD'S GOVERNING RULE. That rule is "cleanup must never
be quieter than what it removed", justified by the fact that ~/.local/state/flywheel/doorbell/*.unanswered
is LOAD-BEARING — gate P2b in ~/.agents/AGENTS.md reads it to decide whether a crew is invisible and
a spawn route is safe. A row-retention prune is the single most direct way to make that file quieter.
The only rows a prune could remove are rows in files for workspaces the daemon no longer hosts, and
those are precisely the frozen mail-only-crew signatures P2b exists to read.

The bead's own mitigation — "if a prune would empty a file the gate reads, REPLACE it with a tombstone
row" — is the right instinct, but it produces a row that is not a pin. Gate P2b is PROSE executed by an
agent, not code, so a `# pruned 2026-09-28` line in that file is a line the reader has to correctly
interpret. Trading "a pin the gate can read" for "a comment the gate must understand" is a downgrade
in the one place the rule says not to go quieter.

WHAT I DID INSTEAD: the fence, because the file had NO TEST AT ALL. save_unanswered/load_unanswered
were untested and this file is what a gate reads. The new test proves the structural claim rather than
asserting it in a comment: a full rewrite drops the pins that stopped being unanswered, with no age
policy and no clock involved.

It also pins a fence against a FUTURE optimisation that would disarm the gate quietly: after
save_unanswered(&[]) the file MUST still exist. P2b reads it by path, and "the daemon looked and found
nothing" is indistinguishable from "the daemon never wrote" if the file is missing. A well-meaning
"skip writing when the list is empty" would convert a clean signal into a missing one. The test asserts
the file exists and reads as empty, and that an unseen workspace reads empty rather than erroring.

WHAT I DID NOT DO, explicitly. No age window. No tombstone rows. No deletion of any .unanswered file,
including the empty ones for dead workspaces (adr22 and flywheel-probe-enametoolong at 37.7 days,
flywheel-flywheel-flywheel at 18.3). Deleting 16 files of ~1 byte each buys nothing measurable, and
existence-versus-rows is the one ambiguity in how P2b is read by a human or an agent; removing the
files would resolve that ambiguity in the direction that loses a signal. If that ambiguity is worth
settling, settle it by making the gate read ROWS rather than presence, in the gate — not by deleting
state under it.

ONE MORE GAP, NOT MINE TO CLOSE HERE. serve.rs:2061 counts journal workspaces with
`!rest.contains('.')`, so a workspace whose name legitimately contains a dot — flywheel-toron.dev is
BOTH a real workspace and a real journal file here — is excluded from the `workspaces` count in
health. That is a count, not a prune, and it undercounts rather than overcounts, so it cannot delete
anything. It is the same shape as the bd-oa4u parse bug and worth a look, but it is not this item.
close_reason: bd-3uqz item D DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT AS SPECIFIED; the deliverable is the fence, because *.unanswered is load-bearing for gate P2b and had no test at all. Re-measured: 16 files, 16 rows total, 12 with zero rows — the bead's 117-row backlog is gone and there was never a per-row leak. Hear::heard and the late-pubkey path both unanswered.remove(pin), and persist_hear rewrites the whole file from the live set every sweep, so a row exists iff the pin is unanswered right now. The spec's own clauses were mutually inconsistent: 'never prune a file that still has live rows' needs per-row ages, and the rows are bare pins with no timestamp, so the policy was not implementable without a format change. A row-retention prune is also the most direct way to make the file quieter, in the one place the governing rule forbids it, and the only rows it could remove are the frozen mail-only-crew signatures P2b exists to read. No age window, no tombstone rows, no deletion of any .unanswered file including the empty ones for dead workspaces: 16 files of ~1 byte buys nothing, and existence-versus-rows is the one ambiguity in how P2b is read — settle it by making the gate read ROWS, in the gate.

principles.name: encode-lessons-in-structure
principles.decision: the rule that binds a close must not be movable by prose about someone else's reservation

title: ADR-0019 binds a bead to the newest commit whose MESSAGE MENTIONS it, so a later lane's prose about a reservation steals the bound revision and reopens complete work
description:
LIVE, measured 2026-09-28 while closing bd-xkte. The work landed at 3fdcff30
with the bead id in its SUBJECT ("... [bd-xkte]") and a gate row bound to it.
One minute later another lane landed fb81e70 ("[bd-3uqz] registry pruning on
POSITIVE evidence of death"), whose BODY mentions my bead exactly once, and only
to say what it was NOT doing:

    NOT WIRED IN, DELIBERATELY. crates/doorbell-rt/src/file_host.rs is reserved
    CopperWren/bd-xkte and carries their in-flight work, so the call site is not
    mine to add.

derive_head_sha walks `git log --all --grep=bd-xkte --format=%H` newest-first and
returns the newest candidate that is not bookkeeping-only. fb81e70 is newer and
is real work, so it became the bound revision. `flywheel ledger check bd-xkte`
then read:

    no legal verdict bound to sha fb81e70... (legal-close table, ADR-0019 Spec 1)
      gate unit-test-verified: note binds sha 3fdcff30..., not the revision fb81e70...

The close-detect loop turns a non-Legal verdict into a reopen, so this reopens a
bead whose work had just landed, passed its gates, and was closed correctly. A
second instance was in flight: 91d0a7b mentions bd-v5r0 the same way and was
harmless only because my commit for bd-v5r0 happened to land one minute LATER.

WHY THIS IS A DESIGN DEFECT AND NOT CARELESSNESS. Two mechanisms pull in
opposite directions:

  1. The pre-commit guard (`toron guard check` -> `bead_hunk_violations`) REQUIRES
     every bd-* token in the ADDED diff lines to appear in the commit message. So
     a commit that merely touches code beside another lane's work MUST cite that
     lane's bead id in order to commit at all.
  2. The ledger binds a bead to the newest commit whose MESSAGE MENTIONS that id.

Honoring (1) breaks (2). fb81e70 was compliant and my binding was the casualty.
Any cross-lane commit that mentions a reservation id is enough, and by the time
derive_head_sha sees it, prose is indistinguishable from a claim of work.

WHAT IT COSTS: a false reopen. ADR-0019 Spec 1 exists so a close can be checked
without trusting the author, and it does work. But when it reopens the wrong
things, everyone learns to treat the check as noise, which is how a real
violation gets waved through later.

PROPOSED FIX, one rule inside derive_head_sha's candidate ranking: PREFER the
commit whose SUBJECT carries the id over one that only mentions it in the body.
Every work commit in this repo writes the id in the subject (`[bd-x] subject` or
`subject [bd-x]`), and the citation debt the guard imposes lands in the BODY.
Ranking subject-carrying commits first, and falling back to body mentions only
when no commit carries the id in its subject, keeps every honest close bound
where it was and stops prose from moving a revision.

Cheaper variant if the ranking is judged too clever: have the guard's required
citation use a distinct token form (`refs bd-x`) that the binder excludes.

RELATED, NOT THE SAME: the guard's tokenizer reads `bd-gpj0.1` as `bd-gpj0`,
because the token body class is [a-z0-9-]+ and a dot terminates it. A dotted
sub-bead id therefore binds a DIFFERENT bead, the parent. Two such citations had
to be removed from added comments during this close rather than hijack bd-gpj0's
revision.

INTERIM MITIGATION APPLIED (loud, not silent, and reversible): bd-xkte now
carries two rows. Row 575 binds 3fdcff30, the commit that carries the work. Row
576 binds derived fb81e70 and says in its own note that it exists only to satisfy
the current rule. When this defect is fixed, row 576 should be retired and the
close re-bound to 3fdcff30.
close_reason: derive_head_sha now ranks subject-carrying commits above body mentions: a later lane commit that only cites the id in prose can no longer steal a close binding, which the pre-commit guard makes unavoidable by requiring every bd-* token in added diff lines to appear in the message. Both fail-closed bails (empty commit, all-bookkeeping) are unchanged. Ran: mbx test -p flywheel --bin flywheel -- derive_head_sha (10 passed); live: the staged binary resolves bd-xkte to the work commit 3fdcff30 where the installed one resolves the sibling fb81e70.

comments.author: CopperWren
comments.text:
SECOND TRIGGER, guaranteed to recur, same rule.

The CHANGELOG [Unreleased] sections cite bead ids in prose (e.g. the
bd-gpj0.1 line). Editing CHANGELOG.md to credit a bead therefore does two
things at once: the guard requires that id in the commit message, and the
commit is real work rather than bookkeeping, so it becomes the newest
candidate and moves every credited bead's derived revision. Writing release
notes for N beads invalidates N closes in one commit.

Evidence: I deliberately did NOT write the three CHANGELOG entries for the
2026-09-28 fixes (bd-v5r0 send race, bd-6bpg ring-test pin, bd-xkte store
skew), precisely because each citation would have re-derived all three
bindings to the changelog commit and demanded verdicts there. The changelog
is now three entries stale on purpose, and that staleness is the cost of the
current rule.

ORDERING CONSEQUENCE: the ranking fix (subject over body mention) should land
BEFORE any release-note pass, or CHANGELOG.md must join the bookkeeping class
alongside .beads/ and .flywheel/. Otherwise the release process itself is the
thief.

principles.name: sequence-verifiable-units
principles.decision: a park/sleep-until step is the missing unit that makes a durable fence re-drivable at T; without it the fence can hand back a park and nothing can resume it

title: toron-workflow: add a park/sleep-until step so a host can act on DispatchAcquire::Park
description:
toron-workflow needs a park/sleep-until step so a host runner can hand "park until T" back and be re-driven at T. This is the missing half of bd-fen3 and the reason flywheel's fence adoption stops short of the durable end state.

ESTABLISHED WHILE ADOPTING THE FENCE (bd-fen3, flywheel commit 1011843). The busy-owner fence is complete and usable as a host API: DispatchPool::try_acquire_for_host(agent, now_ms, claimed_generation) returns DispatchAcquire::{Granted(permit), Park{agent, until_ms, effects}, Refused(effects), CapContention}, and DispatchPool::deadline_wake(agent, now_ms) drives HoldContinued / HoldExpired / FencedStale / Acquired. BusyOwnerEffect::SleepUntilDeadline is documented "Agent busy; host should park until deadline (Resonate sleep)". hold_bound_ms is configurable via DispatchConfig.

WHAT IS MISSING. grep for try_acquire_for_host and DispatchAcquire::Park across crates/toron-workflow/src and crates/toron-mcp/src finds only the definition (dispatch.rs:313) and dispatch.rs's OWN test (dispatch.rs:607). Nothing in the engine calls it. And grep for SleepUntilDeadline under crates/toron-workflow/src/engine/ returns nothing — there is no park step type and no code path that handles the effect. So the fence is a host-side primitive that NO host has adopted, and the engine provides no way to act on a Park result.

WHY IT MATTERS. A workflow that sends more prompts to one agent than it can absorb — wave-swarm puts 7 stages on 3 agents, so 2-3 prompts each — needs to PARK between them, durably. Without an engine park step, a host can only sleep in-process, which is exactly the shape bd-fen3 had to delete: a blocking wait inside a dispatch. bd-5llv showed what that costs: an in-process wait that gives up becomes a retry-exhaustion, and a retry exhaustion opens a breaker. The in-process wait bd-fen3 replaced was itself a workaround for this gap.

SUGGESTED SHAPE, for whoever picks it up. A step or action that consumes a host Park and defers the step rather than failing it: on DispatchAcquire::Park, the scheduler emits the deadline (SleepUntilDeadline already carries until_ms) and re-drives the step after it, calling deadline_wake on wake; HoldContinued re-parks at the SAME deadline without extending the bound window; HoldExpired forks (ForkRebind, generation++) and retries the acquire. That is the Resonate-style sleep the effect's own doc already names.

TWO CONSTRAINTS FROM THE FLYWHEEL SIDE, so the design does not have to be rediscovered. First, DEFAULT_HOLD_BOUND_MS is 10_000, which is far too short for a real agent turn — a multi-minute turn will expire mid-flight and fork. If the engine adopts a park it needs a realistic default or an explicit required config, and it must be documented that HoldContinued does not restart the bound window. Second, the park must be genuinely durable: a crash between Park and the wake must not lose the prompt, and the prompt must not be re-sent to an agent that already holds it (flywheel's state::SentRecord dedup is the current evidence for that, and it is per-process bookkeeping, not durable).

VERIFY by a host that parks and resumes across a process restart, not by a single timed run — a single run cannot distinguish a durable park from a sleep.

title: doorbell afk/digest prints unbounded stale history with epoch timestamps, hiding new wakes
description: FOUND 2026-09-13 while proving bd-cak3 live. 'flywheel doorbell afk flywheel' printed 'doorbell afk digest (362 items)' consisting almost entirely of one repeated old row ('fact-miss -: fact without captain alias: [doorbell] ledger bd-test-close closed') -- and the newest ring, an Audit queued for pin QuietHeron from seconds earlier, was NOT in the output at all. The verb's own help says 'batch captain-relevant wakes since the last digest (ADR-0010 D5)', so the window is not being applied (or no durable 'last digest' watermark exists and it folds from Default every time). Separately the relative-time rendering is wrong: entries print as '[1789285824s ago]' -- a raw epoch value labelled as seconds-ago, i.e. ~56 years. Net effect: the one batch surface a human reads is unreadable noise that omits the fresh wake, so 'the operator can see why they were woken' fails even after the ring itself is correct (bd-cak3). FIX DIRECTION: persist a per-identity/workspace digest watermark and fold only rows after it; cap the batch; render ts as a real relative duration. Repro: run flywheel doorbell afk flywheel and compare against the tail of journals/doorbell-journal-<ws>.jsonl.
close_reason: Captain digest surface made readable and complete. (1) ROOT: afk folded EVERY workspace in the journal dir; the synthetic fact workspaces (manual, facts-close-*, facts-lapsed-*) have no clock-bearing Msg, so their digest drain (workspace.rs drain gated on now-last_digest_unix > interval) never fires and their whole history accumulated -- that is the 376 identical foreign rows. Now folds only the requested project's workspaces via doorbell_scoped_workspaces (shared with why, one definition). (2) TIMESTAMP: at_unix==0 means 'before any clock Msg in this fold'; now-last printed a raw epoch dressed as 's ago' (~56 years). render_digest now prints [age unknown] instead, asserted by bd_z5ut_digest_never_dresses_epoch_zero_as_an_age. (3) BOUNDED: newest --limit (default 100) with the withheld count printed -- a silently truncated digest is the same failure as an unbounded one. (4) COMPLETE: afk now also prints digest-bound wakes read from the journal rows (digest_action_entries), because the embedded fold cannot produce them (no InboxFetched arm = bd-c9jw) -- without this the surface said 'queue empty' while the operator pin's ring sat in the journal, which was the bead's exact complaint. LIVE: 376 foreign rows + fresh wake ABSENT -> 0 foreign rows, 2 real digest-bound wakes with ISO timestamps. Verify: full-suite green, clippy -D warnings clean, 2 new unit tests. PRINCIPLES: fix-root-causes -- the unbounded queue was a workspace-scoping bug, not a rendering one; do-not-claim-unverified -- 'age unknown' beats a number that means nothing.

    profile `scout` (model `@cheap`, declared harness ``) does not route on harness `pi`
    profile `scout` (model `@cheap`, declared harness ``) does not route on harness `omp`
    profile `scout` (model `@cheap`, declared harness ``) does not route on harness `pa`
    profile `scout` (model `@cheap`, declared harness ``) does not route on harness `jcode`
    profile `scout` (model `@cheap`, declared harness ``) does not route on harness `grok`
    profile `scout` (model `@cheap`, declared harness ``) does not route on harness `codex`
    profile `scout` (model `@cheap`, declared harness ``) does not route on harness `claude`
    profile `scout` (model `@cheap`, declared harness ``) does not route on harness `fx`
    ... "no routable model: primary \"opencode/big-pickle\" cannot run on h[arness]"

So scout works on exactly ONE of nine harnesses. It is a BARE-HARNESS profile — the one shape the
operator named explicitly — so this is the exact case the requirement is about.

THE ROOT CAUSE IS A COMMENT THAT IS WRONG, NOT A CAP THAT IS WRONG.

models.rs:774 says:

    `big-pickle` is capped to the `opencode` harness — it is free ONLY there; strict resolution
    refuses it elsewhere (no fallback by design, the scout profile pins the opencode harness).

The cap is correct and deliberate: the model is free on opencode and nowhere else. The LAST CLAUSE
is false. The builtin scout profile is:

    "scout", Profile { harness: String::new(), model: "@cheap".into(), effort: "low".into(), ... }

`harness` is EMPTY, which means scout inherits whatever harness the crew supplies. So the
"no fallback by design" reasoning is built on a pin that does not exist, and the consequence is a
profile that cannot crew eight of the nine registered harnesses.

There is no prior test for this. `resolve_profile_route` has coverage, and
`full_ladder_caps_block_detours_to_model_fallback_then_slot_harness` covers the ladder's ORDER, but
nothing enumerated profiles against harnesses — which is the property the requirement names.

TWO HONEST FIXES, and this one is a COST decision so it is not mine to make silently.

  (a) Make the comment true: set scout's `harness` to `opencode`. Then `@cheap` always resolves and
      the "no fallback by design" clause becomes accurate. The cost: scout can no longer crew a
      claude, codex or grok crew at all, so a crew that pins those harnesses has NO scout. That
      satisfies the comment and violates the requirement.

  (b) Give scout a `model_fallback` to a portable model. `models.toml` already has two with
      `caps = []` — `anthropic/opus-5` and `deepseek/deepseek-v4` — both routable on every harness.
      Then scout works on all nine, which is what the operator asked for. The cost: off opencode a
      scout runs on a paid model rather than a free one, and `@cheap` stops meaning "cheap" on those
      harnesses. Whether a scout is worth an opus is a judgement about the work, not about the code.

My read: (b) matches the stated requirement, and `@cheap` is already only a floor — the slot's own
harness is `pi` for `premium` and the default ladder is separate. But the cost delta is real and the
operator owns it, so this bead records the choice rather than making it.

WHAT IS NOT WRONG AND MUST NOT BE "FIXED": the cap on `big-pickle`. It encodes that the model is
free only on opencode. Emptying `caps` to make the matrix green would delete a cost fact and produce
a green test over a configuration that then bills opencode-model prices on harnesses that cannot run
it. A matrix that is satisfied by deleting the constraint it is testing has measured nothing.

THE MATRIX IS THE DELIVERABLE AND IT IS CURRENTLY RED, deliberately. A guard that reported green over
8 real failures would be worse than no guard. The two companion tests in the same commit are green:
`every_harness_named_by_a_workflow_is_registered` (40 workflows, every harness named anywhere in the
catalog is registered) and `every_slot_harness_and_its_fallback_are_live_registry_entries`. Both carry
their own non-vacuity assertions, because a matrix that enumerates nothing reports green and means
nothing — the bd-hhyl trap, which this session has now hit three separate times.

comments.author: bangedorrunt
comments.text:
OPERATOR DIRECTION received 2026-09-29: 'agent/harness choice should be dynamic/flexible with default'. That is a THIRD option, (c), distinct from the (a)/(b) cost decision this bead parked for the operator. Taking it, and it dissolves the cost question by changing the shape rather than the bill.

WHAT (c) IS. Make the PROFILE path resolve the way the BARE path already does, instead of the profile ladder failing where a bare spawn of the same intent succeeds. This is not a new mechanism: the dynamic default already exists and already has exactly one caller.

THE EVIDENCE FOR THE ROOT CAUSE, which is an ASYMMETRY and not a missing cap.
- bare_model_launch_args (src/main.rs:3822) is the BARE-harness path and ALREADY resolves dynamically: coupled_default_model(harness), then a grok fail-loud, then implied_slot_name_for_harness(..).effective_slot_model(..).
- coupled_default_model (src/models.rs:641) is the generalisation of that idea, and it has exactly ONE caller in the tree - the bare path.
- resolve_profile_route_full (src/models.rs:41) is the PROFILE path and calls NEITHER. Its rungs are: profile pin -> slot -> model_fallback[] -> slot.fallback_harness -> registry ModelEntry.fallback -> fail. Every one of those is a DECLARED name. There is no rung that says 'pick something routable on the harness in hand'.

So scout (harness:'', model:'@cheap') means 'inherit the harness, take the cheap tier' - semantically identical to a bare spawn - yet it is routed through the one path that has no default. That is the bug, and it is why fixing the cap, the comment, or adding a hardcoded fallback each address the wrong thing.

THE 8 FAILURES ARE THREE CLASSES, AND THE BEAD TREATED THEM AS ONE. Splitting them changes the deliverable:
  (i)  pa, jcode, fx  - Open tier, implied_slot: None. A dynamic default is legitimate and is the actual ask.
  (ii) pi, omp         - Open tier, implied slot EXISTS (@standard -> opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor, @premium -> zai/glm-5.3, both portable). The profile path simply never consults it. A pure gap.
  (iii) grok, codex, claude - CLOSED tier.

CLASS (iii) MUST NOT BE 'FIXED', and this is the load-bearing correction. HarnessTier::Closed is documented in src/harness_registry.rs:25 as 'Frontier CLI with its own model. Never asked for one', may_be_asked_for_a_model() is false for it, and coupled_default_model deliberately returns None for a coupled harness with no registered family id so the caller fails loud (bd-ovew: never a foreign-provider id). Handing codex or claude a zai/* id to make the matrix green would be the same class of error as emptying the caps: deleting a constraint instead of satisfying a requirement. grok is additionally required to FAIL LOUD.

So 'all 9 route' is not the requirement - it is an over-broad restatement of it, and the matrix test encodes it. The real requirement is: every OPEN-tier harness routes, dynamically, with a named default; every CLOSED-tier harness refuses, loudly and for the right reason. A test demanding 9/9 cannot distinguish those and would reward exactly the wrong fix.

COST, HONESTLY. Every registered model reports cost_in_per_mtok = 0.0 - there is NO cost data in the registry at all. So a 'cheapest routable model' ordering would be a fabricated cost fact, the same class of error as the context-length conclusion I retracted on bd-7wah. The dynamic rung therefore does NOT claim to optimise cost: it prefers the same provider family as the tier's intent, then falls back to a deterministic ordered pick, and the route step is NAMED so the choice is visible in the ledger rather than silent.

title: watch-read test pins a store behavior that bd-asbc has since fixed
description:
`a_thread_scoped_read_survives_a_limit_smaller_than_the_inbox` deliberately characterized the store returning the OLDEST rows under a limit, so the thread-scoping fix would not sit there unnoticed as cargo cult. bd-asbc fixed the store, so the characterization now fails: an un-scoped read correctly returns the newest rows.

The test must pin the two live contracts rather than a fixed bug:
1. the store window is newest-N, so a regression there surfaces here as a failed test instead of a mystery collab timeout;
2. a thread-scoped read returns that thread newest rows under a limit smaller than the whole inbox, i.e. the thread filter is applied BEFORE the limit.

Contract 2 needs send order where the newest rows overall are NOT in the watched thread, otherwise the scoped and un-scoped reads return the same thing and the test can no longer tell scoping from the store window.

The production fix is unchanged and still correct: `cmd_mail_watch` scopes its read, which is what makes it independent of the store window.

## PRINCIPLES
prove-it-works — a test that encodes a bug as expected behavior is a time bomb; pin the contract, not the defect.

## VERIFY
```bash
mbx +nightly-aarch64-apple-darwin test -p flywheel --bin flywheel -- a_thread_scoped_read_survives
```
close_reason: prove-it-works — a characterization of a known bug is a time bomb the moment the bug is fixed, so the test now pins both live contracts and the send order is chosen so scoping cannot be confused with the store window.
